item.title: ‘Everyone needs to take a deep breath and slow down,’ says Pammy Hutton
item.dc:content:
Once upon a time, a mother was leading her seven-year-old daughter on her pony. A bird flew out of a bush; the child wobbled off, broke her neck and was paralysed.

Riding is frequently listed among high-risk sports, up there with motorsports. The obvious solution is to mitigate that risk and, indeed, equestrians have access to good safety gear.

Not so easy to address is the unpredictability of horses and what’s going on in the vicinity when riding one. So, even as we don full body armour, are we neglecting other aspects of safety?

It’s never worth intentionally risking life, however much you love the horse or however good a rider you think you are. My late mother, Mrs Molly Sivewright, a renowned expert in riding-related court cases, taught me how risk-taking ruins families, causing grief like nobody can imagine.

Having myself lost a child through a cot death, I know how fleeting life can be. Yet online I watch more and more equestrian accidents waiting to happen.

Some riders specialise too much and too soon, so they lack wide-ranging equestrian skills in different environments and over varied terrain. Likewise, some horses are trained too intensely in one discipline and thus have too narrow an education. Neither group knows how to cope in the “real world”.

How long before there’s a major accident in para dressage? Or a manslaughter charge is launched?

Horses are not robots and the overuse of calmers cannot be advocated. Of course, riding helps with disabilities, mentally and physically, but safety is paramount.

As the quest for winning equine-machines continues, and with 80% scores now required to win at Paralympic level, it’s bordering on dangerous. I worry particularly for the newer-to-the-sport nations who might try to buy medals with money, yet don’t have the safeguarding experience of more seasoned countries.

Also concerning me is how many good riders and eminent coaches post videos of schooling and teaching with arena gates and doors wide open. Clearly, riders need to enter and leave a school, but other riders should stay 10m away.

Once, while riding at a workshop, I was passing the door in counter-canter when someone opened it. My horse shot through, badly damaging my leg.

Overall, being in a hurry around horses causes many a mishap. Everyone needs to take a deep breath and slow down. Think of it as an “interval training” lifestyle.

The BHS route

How does our current British Horse Society (BHS) educational system get on the ladder for government funding by 2028 to enable school-leavers to train within the horse industry?

Students can choose GCSE PE or BTEC sport and use riding as one of their sports. However, if a student opts for a sport outside mainstream education, most schools offer little or no support in terms of guidance, facilitation or financial help.

The new government policy is “to assist young people into hard or soft hats”. The challenge is getting “equine” recognised as a valued place for training.

The BHS system is globally renowned, saluted as a prized training structure and a vital part of the equine education landscape for all ages. We must ensure it remains so for future generations.

Recently, there’s been much media attention to “new” coaching qualifications under the British Equestrian banner. They are not actually new; I did the dressage version several years ago! Each of the disciplines can now offer a unified coaching qualification that enables candidates to move from one sport to another, provided they then complete the technical qualification offered by their new sport.

Yet BHS qualifications remain the only route to a) assess competence in riding, coaching and horse care, and b) enable candidates to progress to a Fellowship (FBHS), which is widely acknowledged as the world’s highest qualification.

Like BHS qualifications, the British Equestrian Coaching Certificate will be on the national framework for qualifications, therefore ultimately regulated by government. But I still hang my hat on the BHS system because it’s all-encompassing.

Many elite coaches involved in international sport are FBHSs. Aspiring coaches with long-term goals are advised to plan their route accordingly.

● Which route into coaching and the horse industry do you think best prepares young people, and why? Let us know your thoughts at hhletters@futurenet.com, including your name, nearest town and county, for the chance to have your thoughts published in a future issue of Horse & Hound magazine

item.title: Top stud ‘deeply devastated’ after broodmares attacked and killed – €10,000 reward for information
item.dc:content:
Three horses have died and three others have been injured following attacks at Schockemöhle stud farm in Germany.

Police are investigating following the incidents, involving predominantly pregnant broodmares, between 11 September and 11 October.

“At our stud farm, serious incidents have occurred in which several of our horses on the outer pastures were severely injured and tragically died,” said a Schockemöhle stud spokesperson today (21 October).

“The police have been intensively investigating this case for a long time. Based on the explicit recommendation of the investigating authorities, we are now appealing to the public in order to reach potential witnesses and gather further information.”

The spokesperson added that the “loss of our horses and the circumstances of their deaths have left us deeply devastated”. The stud has offered a €10,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of the perpetrator(s).

“This makes it all the more important to us that these events are fully investigated and resolved,” he said.

“We thank everyone who supports us in this investigation and can assist with information.”

A police statement today said the Schwerin criminal police inspectorate and public prosecutor’s office are conducting extensive investigations.

“Numerous employees of the affected stud farm will be questioned today,” read the statement.

“A total of six horses have been attacked so far, three of which have died. The affected horses were predominantly pregnant broodmares with a value of several tens of thousands of euros.”

The statement added that police are investigating “on suspicion of violations of the Animal Welfare Act and property damage”.

A police spokesperson told H&H that due to the ongoing investigation no further details could be provided, but confirmed the incidents took place between 11 September and 11 October, “predominantly at weekends”.

Anyone with information or who witnessed unusual activity around the stud’s pastures in recent weeks is asked to contact Schwerin Police (0049 0385 51804801 or by visiting https://portal.onlinewache.polizei.de/de/).

item.dc:creator: Becky Murray
item.dc:description: <p>Becky Murray started freelance writing for <em>Horse & Hound</em> in 2016 alongside other equestrian titles, before joining the <em>H&H</em> news team in July 2018. She moved up to senior news writer in January 2022. During her time at <em>H&H</em> she has reported on a broad range of topics across the equestrian industry including welfare issues, veterinary studies, FEI Tribunal hearings, rider safety, and road safety campaigns. In 2019 she attended the national Strangles Symposium and the Scottish welfare conference.</p><p>Becky was part of the home remote reporting team for the Tokyo and Paris Olympic Games as well as multiple European Championships. She has reported in person from Morris Equestrian, the Royal Highland Show, Blair Castle, Scone Palace and Luhmühlen. She is attending the 2025 European Para Dressage Championships as Horse & Hound’s on-site reporter.</p><p>Based in north Scotland, Becky learnt to ride at the age of five. She got the showjumping bug with her 13.2hh older pony Phoenix, who used to particularly enjoy a chase-me-Charlie. She went on to compete in British Showjumping and riding club activities as a teenager with her pony Sparkle. After losing two horses in 2015 to illness and injury, Becky is now producing two Irish mares, Ruby and Chloe, and hopes to get back in the showjumping ring in the future. She also has two miniature Shetland sisters, Mootie and Poppet, who keep her on her toes.</p>

item.title: Fresh look for dressage championships, plus a new ‘best of British’ concept
item.dc:content:
A change of venue, different dates and a new concept are on the cards for 2027 as part of British Dressage’s (BD) overhaul of its championships.

The 2027 BD National Championships, held at Somerford Park for the last six years and Stoneleigh before that, will move to Hartpury and will be brought forward two weeks to the end of August, rebranded as the Summer Championships.

BD is also creating a new British Masters initiative to “celebrate the best of British dressage at international level”, which will run at Wellington Riding in June, as part of the existing CDI and CPEDI fixture. It will be open to all BD members who are FEI registered.

Points will be awarded to the top five in each category and, British Masters champions will be crowned at grand prix, small tour, under-25, youth age groups and para (all grades).

At the 2026 BD AGM, chief executive Jason Brautigam said BD has been “reviewing the commercial viability of the national championships in its current form over the last few years”.

He added that Somerford Park has provided “a wonderful home to the nationals”, and that BD is “enormously grateful for the generous support of the King family”, and thanked Kelvin Bywater and his team at Show Direct.

“Escalating costs and declining attendance have obviously made it a challenging event to run on a greenfield site, where we need to bring in temporary infrastructure, power, and facilities,” he said, adding that the format will change from a paid spectator event to a competitor show.

“We’re aiming to mirror the model we've used successfully for the Winter Championships, where admission is free for all spectators and live streaming available for all classes. This will ensure that the event continues to thrive long term, encouraging greater attendance, enhancing media coverage and providing an increased profile for our competitors, our partners and our sponsors.”

Mr Brautigam said one of the drawbacks of having the nationals in September is that this is after the international season finishes, so “we rarely get to see top British combinations compete”. This led to the idea for the British Masters.

“The event will have a strong British heritage feel and will be a spectator-friendly show with trade stands and hospitality, and people will be able to watch top combinations competing for selection for the major international championships,” he said.

H&H columnist Richard Davison said he loved the championships at Somerford, that it had a “fantastic atmosphere” there, and he is sad to see it move.

“But if it's not viable because of all the extra tentage and temporary facilities they need, I understand the need to innovate and keep trying other venues,” he said.

He added that it is “fabulous” that BD will run the British Masters across so many levels.

“The British Masters is a really interesting concept; the dressage community do like seeing our team horses. The governing body has to bear in mind that, especially in respect of horses based abroad, there will always be exceptions to whether those horses can attend,” he said, adding that he would therefore caution against this developing into a compulsory selection trial.

Fellow H&H columnist Anna Ross said past championships have been great and – without taking anything away from them – she welcomes the news about the new fixtures.

“What I would like to see, and what I think was a really nice part of when the championships were at Stoneleigh, is the two arenas next to each other,” she told H&H.

“Sometimes that could be frustrating – I remember nearly falling off once when the crowd started clapping for the other competitor! – but if they could coordinate the timing, there is nothing more inspiring for a young person than riding into the arena at the same time as a member of the British team. Everybody being in there together really is the spirit of that championship.”

She said she “loves” the British Masters idea, adding that the Wellington show is already top quality, and for fans to have the chance to see likely team contenders just before they go to international championships “will make everybody feel more part of it”.

“Then we’ll have the Summer Championships to look forward to, I think it will be a really nice bounce from one to the next – everyone will have fired up their inspiration to go and knock it out of the park,” she said.

● What do you think? Let us know your thoughts at hhletters@futurenet.com, including your name, nearest town and county, for the chance to have your thoughts published in a future issue of Horse & Hound magazine

item.dc:creator: Lucy Elder
item.dc:description: <p>Lucy joined the <em>H&H</em> newsdesk in 2015, taking on the senior news writer position in 2018.</p><p>Since joining the <em>Horse & Hound</em> team, Lucy has interviewed many top riders and has reported on the ground from major global sporting events including the Tokyo Paralympic Games and multiple European Championships. She has also reported at countless other national and international fixtures, in the UK and abroad, including Burghley, Badminton and London, and has been part of the remote coverage team for Olympics and world championships.</p><p>Her news writing experience includes covering current affairs and sports news across the spectrum of equestrian disciplines and racing, as well as human and equine welfare, industry news and court cases.</p><p>Lucy grew up as a member of the Belvoir Hunt branch of the Pony Club and competed up to intermediate level eventing. She spent a year working in eventing yards before university, where she became a member of the Great Britain Student Riders squad and competed in Ireland, Spain and Germany.</p><p>After graduating from <a href="https://www.brookes.ac.uk/" target="_blank">Oxford Brookes</a> in 2012, Lucy trained as a journalist at <a href="https://newsassociates.co.uk/" target="_blank">News Associates</a> in London where she received her NCTJ (National Council for the Training of Journalists) qualification. She spent two years as a news reporter and entertainment editor on the <a href="https://www.windsorexpress.co.uk/" target="_blank"><em>Windsor Express</em></a>, <a href="https://www.sloughexpress.co.uk/" target="_blank"><em>Slough Express</em></a> and <a href="https://www.maidenhead-advertiser.co.uk/" target="_blank"><em>Maidenhead Advertiser</em></a> titles at Baylis Media, passing her senior NQJ (National Qualification in Journalism) exams in 2015 and joining <em>H&H</em> the same year.</p><p>In 2018, Lucy received the British Equestrian Federation’s journalist of the year award, which recognises “great journalism in equestrian sport, celebrating the work of a written journalist, broadcaster or photographer who has gone above and beyond to promote equestrian sport during the past year”. She has twice reached the shortlist for the Martin Wills Writing Awards (2013 and 2014), for writing on a racing theme, and is also vice-chairman of the <a href="https://bema.org.uk/" target="_blank">British Equestrian Media Association</a>.</p>

item.title: New FEI grand prix dressage test unveils highly anticipated changes – H&H’s dressage editor explains the new tests, movement by movement
item.dc:content:
For the first time, grand prix horses will have to stretch on a long rein in trot, as part of the new grand prix test that comes into force on 1 January 2027.

The stretch circle is one of a series of changes in the FEI’s revised dressage tests. They also add stretching and give-and-retake exercises at almost every level below grand prix, from children up to the small tour.

The changes were trialled in Warendorf, Germany, earlier this year. The new tests come into use on the same day the qualification period for minimum eligibility requirements (MERs) for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games opens.

We’ve broken down all the changes riders need to know below.

At a glance

  • Grand prix: a new 20m stretch circle in trot with a coefficient of two, a new route for the walk, and 34 movements instead of 33.
  • Grand prix special: officially “unchanged”, but there is a new give and retake of the reins in canter.
  • Collective mark: renamed from “harmony” to “harmonious riding” in the grand prix and special.
  • Stretch circles and give and retakes have been added to tests from children’s level to the small tour.
  • Medium tour: a new grand prix A for CDI2* shows.
  • Young horses: five-, six- and seven-year-olds now have two preliminary tests.
  • World Cup: the new grand prix will be used at all CDI-W shows from 1 January 2027.

Grand prix

The FEI describes the changes as minor, but for riders, the stretch circle is a significant new demand.

After the canter work, riders trot a 20m circle right from R, and may sit or rise. Between R and S they let the horse stretch on a long rein. Between S and R they retake the reins and return to sitting trot.

The circle carries a coefficient of two. Judges will be looking for:

  • rhythm and balance being maintained
  • a gradual forward and downward stretch of the neck
  • the reins being retaken without resistance
  • an accurate circle

The change will be welcomed by H&H columnist Carl Hester, who has called for a stretch at grand prix level since autumn 2024. That was when he backed Kyra Kyrklund’s idea of bringing the young horse tests’ give and retake of the reins into the PSG and grand prix, describing it later as “a brilliant idea.”

Writing this spring, Carl said that “horses stretch a lot better in rising trot” and hoped the choice would be left to riders. The new test gives them that choice.

The middle of the test has also been rerouted. According to the FEI, the extended walk follows a new line so that judges get a clearer view of the subsequent collected walk. This has a knock-on effect on the passage–piaffe tour that follows.

The test now has 34 movements, and the total scored marks rise from 460 to 480. Despite the extra movement, the suggested time given on the sheet – which is for information only – falls from 6min 30sec to 5min 55sec.

The minimum age for grand prix horses remains eight. However, the FEI told H&H that the minimum age for grand prix at five-star and championship level is being discussed as part of its current rules revision.

Movement by movement, here’s what has changed:

Movements 1 to 10 are unchanged. However, the collected trot on the short side after the first extended trot is now spelled out in the directive ideas for movement 2.

Movement 11, the extended walk, now runs from P to S rather than from P to H, and still has a coefficient of two.

Movement 12, the collected walk, starts as the rider approaches H. Riders then turn right at H and cross the arena through G to M, instead of going round the short side via C. It also keeps its coefficient of two.

Movement 13: passage now begins at R rather than M.

Movement 14: passage from R to B, then a turn across to X. In the old test, riders turned at R and rode to I.

Movements 15 and 16: the second piaffe and its transitions are now at X rather than I. That means two of the test’s three piaffes are now ridden at X.

Movement 17: passage from X to E to V, replacing the old line from I to S to E.

Movement 18: the canter strike-off now comes at V rather than E.

Movements 19 to 27 are unchanged.

Movement 28 is the new stretch circle.

Movements 29 to 34 are the old movements 28 to 33, unchanged.

The directive ideas have been reworded throughout. Piaffes and their transitions are now judged on whether they are shown “at the required marker.” The pirouettes no longer specify six to eight strides, and ask for the “correct number of strides”.

Grand prix special

The FEI’s own summary says the grand prix special is unchanged, but riders who learn the test from that will be caught out.

The FEI has confirmed to H&H that the final version of the 2027 special includes a new give and retake of the reins.

In movement 21, riders still strike off into right canter at X. Now, on the following short side, they must give and retake the reins for three to four canter strides. Judges will be looking for a “clear release of rein contact” and “independence of seat”.

Unlike the stretch circle in the grand prix, this isn’t a separate movement. It carries no coefficient and forms part of the mark for the canter transition. The test still has 36 movements and a maximum of 470 marks.

The FEI considered moving the start of the collected walk from S to E. It decided against it, because it felt the change would make both walks harder for the judge at E to assess.

Collective marks renamed

In both the grand prix and the special, the collective mark has been renamed from “harmony” to “harmonious riding”. The description is unchanged (harmony, cooperation, lightness, effectiveness and sensitivity of the aids, and adherence to the training scale), and it still carries a coefficient of two.

It’s a small change, but it feels significant. “Harmony” could describe the partnership as a whole, whereas “harmonious riding” puts the focus squarely on the rider and how the horse is being ridden.

“Harmonious riding” puts the focus squarely on the rider

The collective mark has been renamed

Stretching across the levels

The new exercises are not limited to grand prix:

Small tour: The PSG adds a stretch circle, ridden sitting or rising, and the inter I adds a give and retake of the reins.

Young riders: The team test adds a stretch circle, and the individual test adds a give and retake at the end.

Juniors: A new preliminary test for regions where the sport is developing finishes with a stretch circle.

Ponies: The individual test now includes a stretch circle and a rein back.

Children: Preliminary A adds a give and retake of the reins in trot, and preliminary B adds a stretch circle.

At medium tour level, a new grand prix A has been introduced for CDI2* shows. The current intermediate A and B tests are replaced by intermediate II A and intermediate II B.

Young horses

Five-, six- and seven-year-olds now have two tests.

Preliminary A is a simplified test aimed at regions where young horse training is less established. It cannot be used for MERs or at the World Breeding Championships for Young Horses.

Preliminary B is used at those championships and their qualifiers, alongside the final tests.

The six-year-old preliminary B now includes a stretch circle. This means every horse at the championships shows one, not just those that reach the final.

In the seven-year-old final, the stretch circle can now be ridden sitting or rising, and it carries a coefficient for the first time.

A new grand prix has also been introduced for horses aged eight to 11, for national competitions.

What next?

Riders have until the end of the year to get to grips with the changes. We’re awaiting news from British Dressage on how the new tests will be incorporated at the national level.

For some, the switch will come mid-season. The FEI has confirmed that the new grand prix will be used at all World Cup (CDI-W) shows from 1 January 2027, partway through the 2026/27 World Cup season. But it shouldn’t make too much of a difference – at World Cup shows, the grand prix serves as the qualifier for the freestyle, and standings points are awarded only on the freestyle results.

All the new tests can be downloaded from the FEI website.

item.description: From a new stretch circle to a renamed collective mark, here’s everything riders and spectators need to know about the FEI’s revised dressage tests, which come into effect from 1 January 2027
item.dc:creator: Oscar Williams
item.dc:description: <p>Oscar joined <em>Horse & Hound</em> in October 2023 and is the magazine’s dressage editor and sports manager, overseeing coverage of equestrian sport.</p><p>Raised in Lancashire, Oscar started riding aged 12 and quickly became hooked. A keen member of the Lancaster & District branch of the Pony Club, he learnt to ride on a succession of hand-me-down ponies before persuading his parents to buy him his own horse – a wholly unsuitable but much-loved Welsh section C.</p><p>Oscar went on to study equine science at Myerscough College and, after deciding jumping wasn’t his strong suit, turned to dressage. Inspired by the London 2012 Olympics, he later spent four years working for leading trainer Emile Faurie. During that time, he competed at the 2015 National Dressage Championships and travelled with the yard to CDIs at Aachen, Vidauban, Saumur and Achleiten.</p><p>He also holds a master’s degree in Literature from York St John University (2021), combining his equestrian background with a passion for writing about the sport.</p><p>He regularly reports on elite dressage, breeding and welfare issues, as well as the science and policy shaping modern equestrian sport.</p><p>Oscar now lives in Cumbria with his two boisterous spaniels, Miffy and Dougal, and is interested in making equestrian sport more inclusive and accessible.</p>

item.content:encoded:
For the first time, grand prix horses will have to stretch on a long rein in trot, as part of the new grand prix test that comes into force on 1 January 2027.

The stretch circle is one of a series of changes in the FEI’s revised dressage tests. They also add stretching and give-and-retake exercises at almost every level below grand prix, from children up to the small tour.

The changes were trialled in Warendorf, Germany, earlier this year. The new tests come into use on the same day the qualification period for minimum eligibility requirements (MERs) for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games opens.

We’ve broken down all the changes riders need to know below.

At a glance

  • Grand prix: a new 20m stretch circle in trot with a coefficient of two, a new route for the walk, and 34 movements instead of 33.
  • Grand prix special: officially “unchanged”, but there is a new give and retake of the reins in canter.
  • Collective mark: renamed from “harmony” to “harmonious riding” in the grand prix and special.
  • Stretch circles and give and retakes have been added to tests from children’s level to the small tour.
  • Medium tour: a new grand prix A for CDI2* shows.
  • Young horses: five-, six- and seven-year-olds now have two preliminary tests.
  • World Cup: the new grand prix will be used at all CDI-W shows from 1 January 2027.

Grand prix

The FEI describes the changes as minor, but for riders, the stretch circle is a significant new demand.

After the canter work, riders trot a 20m circle right from R, and may sit or rise. Between R and S they let the horse stretch on a long rein. Between S and R they retake the reins and return to sitting trot.

The circle carries a coefficient of two. Judges will be looking for:

  • rhythm and balance being maintained
  • a gradual forward and downward stretch of the neck
  • the reins being retaken without resistance
  • an accurate circle

The change will be welcomed by H&H columnist Carl Hester, who has called for a stretch at grand prix level since autumn 2024. That was when he backed Kyra Kyrklund’s idea of bringing the young horse tests’ give and retake of the reins into the PSG and grand prix, describing it later as “a brilliant idea.”

Writing this spring, Carl said that “horses stretch a lot better in rising trot” and hoped the choice would be left to riders. The new test gives them that choice.

The middle of the test has also been rerouted. According to the FEI, the extended walk follows a new line so that judges get a clearer view of the subsequent collected walk. This has a knock-on effect on the passage–piaffe tour that follows.

The test now has 34 movements, and the total scored marks rise from 460 to 480. Despite the extra movement, the suggested time given on the sheet – which is for information only – falls from 6min 30sec to 5min 55sec.

The minimum age for grand prix horses remains eight. However, the FEI told H&H that the minimum age for grand prix at five-star and championship level is being discussed as part of its current rules revision.

Movement by movement, here’s what has changed:

Movements 1 to 10 are unchanged. However, the collected trot on the short side after the first extended trot is now spelled out in the directive ideas for movement 2.

Movement 11, the extended walk, now runs from P to S rather than from P to H, and still has a coefficient of two.

Movement 12, the collected walk, starts as the rider approaches H. Riders then turn right at H and cross the arena through G to M, instead of going round the short side via C. It also keeps its coefficient of two.

Movement 13: passage now begins at R rather than M.

Movement 14: passage from R to B, then a turn across to X. In the old test, riders turned at R and rode to I.

Movements 15 and 16: the second piaffe and its transitions are now at X rather than I. That means two of the test’s three piaffes are now ridden at X.

Movement 17: passage from X to E to V, replacing the old line from I to S to E.

Movement 18: the canter strike-off now comes at V rather than E.

Movements 19 to 27 are unchanged.

Movement 28 is the new stretch circle.

Movements 29 to 34 are the old movements 28 to 33, unchanged.

The directive ideas have been reworded throughout. Piaffes and their transitions are now judged on whether they are shown “at the required marker.” The pirouettes no longer specify six to eight strides, and ask for the “correct number of strides”.

Grand prix special

The FEI’s own summary says the grand prix special is unchanged, but riders who learn the test from that will be caught out.

The FEI has confirmed to H&H that the final version of the 2027 special includes a new give and retake of the reins.

In movement 21, riders still strike off into right canter at X. Now, on the following short side, they must give and retake the reins for three to four canter strides. Judges will be looking for a “clear release of rein contact” and “independence of seat”.

Unlike the stretch circle in the grand prix, this isn’t a separate movement. It carries no coefficient and forms part of the mark for the canter transition. The test still has 36 movements and a maximum of 470 marks.

The FEI considered moving the start of the collected walk from S to E. It decided against it, because it felt the change would make both walks harder for the judge at E to assess.

Collective marks renamed

In both the grand prix and the special, the collective mark has been renamed from “harmony” to “harmonious riding”. The description is unchanged (harmony, cooperation, lightness, effectiveness and sensitivity of the aids, and adherence to the training scale), and it still carries a coefficient of two.

It’s a small change, but it feels significant. “Harmony” could describe the partnership as a whole, whereas “harmonious riding” puts the focus squarely on the rider and how the horse is being ridden.

“Harmonious riding” puts the focus squarely on the rider

The collective mark has been renamed

Stretching across the levels

The new exercises are not limited to grand prix:

Small tour: The PSG adds a stretch circle, ridden sitting or rising, and the inter I adds a give and retake of the reins.

Young riders: The team test adds a stretch circle, and the individual test adds a give and retake at the end.

Juniors: A new preliminary test for regions where the sport is developing finishes with a stretch circle.

Ponies: The individual test now includes a stretch circle and a rein back.

Children: Preliminary A adds a give and retake of the reins in trot, and preliminary B adds a stretch circle.

At medium tour level, a new grand prix A has been introduced for CDI2* shows. The current intermediate A and B tests are replaced by intermediate II A and intermediate II B.

Five-, six- and seven-year-olds now have two tests.

Preliminary A is a simplified test aimed at regions where young horse training is less established. It cannot be used for MERs or at the World Breeding Championships for Young Horses.

Preliminary B is used at those championships and their qualifiers, alongside the final tests.

The six-year-old preliminary B now includes a stretch circle. This means every horse at the championships shows one, not just those that reach the final.

In the seven-year-old final, the stretch circle can now be ridden sitting or rising, and it carries a coefficient for the first time.

A new grand prix has also been introduced for horses aged eight to 11, for national competitions.

What next?

Riders have until the end of the year to get to grips with the changes. We’re awaiting news from British Dressage on how the new tests will be incorporated at the national level.

For some, the switch will come mid-season. The FEI has confirmed that the new grand prix will be used at all World Cup (CDI-W) shows from 1 January 2027, partway through the 2026/27 World Cup season. But it shouldn’t make too much of a difference – at World Cup shows, the grand prix serves as the qualifier for the freestyle, and standings points are awarded only on the freestyle results.

All the new tests can be downloaded from the FEI website.

● What do you think of the new grand prix test and will the stretch circle make a difference to how horses are trained and judged? item.title: Why did British horse sport fans have to pay to watch the World Championships in Aachen?
item.dc:content:
The FEI and ClipMyHorse.TV have spoken up to explain their ambition to market horse sport to as many fans as possible – and the barriers to achieving it.

For the UK audience, the action from the World Championships in Aachen this year (11–23 August) was shown solely on ClipMyHorse, a paid-for subscription-only service.

There was a 26% discount for new and returning customers who signed up for the worlds, which meant a year’s access to all ClipMyHorse content for about £154, compared to the normal UK price of around £208. In some countries, the action was on free-to-view television, because national broadcasters had bought the rights.

Previously, international action was streamed on FEI TV but this was integrated into ClipMyHorse and the FEI is a shareholder in the company.

“ClipMyHorse.TV operates primarily as a subscription service, which enables us to fund and deliver comprehensive, high-quality coverage,” ClipMyHorse CEO Markus Detering told H&H.

“For the World Championships, the FEI managed to secure free-to-air [FTA] broadcast deals for certain content in a few key territories. Where live coverage sat within our platform, we aimed to keep as many fans connected as possible by providing select free content, such as our daily highlight show, and pointing viewers toward local FTA broadcasts whenever available.”

Many readers contacted H&H to raise the fact the action was not free to watch in Britain.

Jackie Davies said: “The American news channel CNBC has been showing reasonably full highlights on a Sunday lunchtime. Due to the complete lack of coverage on any UK channel, I am extremely grateful. I do agree with the comment that ClipMyHorse missed out on a revenue stream due to them wanting a full year’s payment and not allowing just for a couple of weeks.”

Others agreed, stating that they would have paid for a shorter subscription just to watch the worlds.

“Your feedback regarding short-term passes and flexible access is very welcome,” Mr Detering told H&H. “As part of our close partnership, ClipMyHorse.TV and the FEI are continuously discussing how we can evolve our broadcasting approach.

“While our foundation remains a subscription-based model, we are already taking steps to increase free accessibility – for example, through our free 24/7 channel on our website, where we plan to feature increasingly exciting content. We are jointly exploring ways to potentially offer more flexible options and broader access.

“Our shared objective with the FEI remains growing the reach and visibility of equestrian sports worldwide. With over 2,000 events broadcast each year, we are fully committed to bringing the sport to as wide an audience as possible.”

Readers told H&H they felt the FEI should have done more to promote horse sport to audiences, and a spokesperson for the federation said the FEI understands this feeling.

“The FEI absolutely shares the ambition to see equestrian sport reach a wider audience, and promoting the sport and making our major events as visible and accessible as possible is a key priority,” she said. “There are, however, a number of challenges in achieving this, particularly for major international events.”

She explained that broadcasting an event of this scale is a “significant undertaking” that comes with extensive production, technical and distribution costs.

Finding the balance

“There is a balance to be found between making content as widely accessible as possible and ensuring there is a sustainable commercial model that can support the level and quality of coverage fans expect,” she said, adding that another challenge is that broadcast rights vary by country, explaining the FTA access in some.

“While the FEI works actively to maximise the visibility of its championships and other events, we operate within a wider media rights landscape in which broadcasters, platforms and rights-holders all have a role to play.”

But, she added, the FEI takes all feedback about accessibility to the sport very seriously.

“The incredible performances at the World Championships are exactly the kind of moments that can introduce new audiences to equestrian sport and inspire existing fans to engage even more closely with it,” she said.

“For us, the challenge is therefore not simply about choosing between ‘free’ and ‘paid’ coverage. It is about finding sustainable ways of bringing the sport to as many people as possible, across different markets and platforms, while continuing to invest in the quality of the coverage itself. This is something we continue to discuss and review with our media partners, including ClipMyHorse.TV.”

  • To stay up to date with the latest equestrian news, subscribe to the Horse & Hound website
item.description: The FEI and ClipMyHorse.TV have explained why the action was covered as it was, and their ambition to promote horse sport as much as possible
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Jones
item.dc:description: <p>Eleanor joined <em>Horse & Hound</em> as news editor in March 2016, having spent eight and a half years working for local and national newspapers. During her time with <em>H&H</em>, Eleanor has attended numerous industry conferences and events, including the FEI sport forum, the British Equine Veterinary Association annual congress and the National Equine Forum, and has spoken at the NEF and the Saddle Research Trust conference. </p><p>She has reported on all disciplines and aspects of the industry, from Brexit to anti-bullying campaigns and from dressage rules to dressage mules. She spent time travelling across Europe with World Horse Welfare to see first-hand the experience of horses being transported thousands of miles to slaughter, producing reports for print, online and in video format, and has also reported on showjumping events from national qualifiers to international grands prix, as well as the 2021, 2023 and 2025 Europeans and 2022 World Championships.</p><p>Eleanor has been riding since she was seven, and was given her first pony, a £300 Welsh section B mare, at the age of 12. She worked for dressage and showjumping riders, and now has two warmblood mares who she competes at British Showjumping events, and two home-bred youngsters. She has competed in dressage but since her mark sheets have contained phrases such as “unexpected manoeuvre between C and M” and “well sat”, tends to stick to the jumping.</p>

item.title: ‘It’s been a few weeks and I’ve been licking my wounds,’ admits Laura Tomlinson after the nationals
item.dc:content:
It has been a few weeks since the LeMieux National Dressage Championships at Somerford Park but I am still licking my wounds! Having had the most incredible start with a win in the prix st georges and inter I, I hit the ground with a serious bump in the grand prix when my high hopes were drowned in the deluge.

Warming up Full Moon II (Moony), I wasn’t too worried as we have all dealt with riding in English downpours. The unexpected aspect was that as I was trotting around the arena before starting, the spectators from the uncovered stands rushed to the covered stands and the judges flicked their headlights and wipers on.

This was game over for Moony. He went backwards more than forwards and spent most of the test trying to convince me that we should run, while I tried to convince him that we needed to stay and finish the job. We had our lowest score ever and I went home early a little perplexed at how the week had turned.

Forest Hill had an OK test, but is new to this level. Although he had qualified for the freestyle, I had nothing prepared. I had never imagined that Moony wouldn’t qualify and you are only allowed to ride one in the freestyle.

My family were delighted that I was back early, armed with a lesson on the ups and downs with horses. I spent Sunday watching my youngest two children showjumping in the rain, winning more rosettes than me.

I had, however, left Somerford feeling excited, too. It is always a privilege to compete at such a well-organised show with fantastic sponsors. My upcoming eight-year-old, Ostmarks Digal (pictured top), had also made me smile, after his two wins. He will compete at Horse of the Year Show in the future elite class, his first ever freestyle [which he won].

In the meantime, Moony and I are regaining confidence and ironing out blips at local shows, as I am convinced that the outside circumstances would not have been so catastrophic for Digal or Forest, who are both less dramatic.

Let’s use the full range of marks

The evening celebrating the life of the late Stephen Clarke was emotional and yet lovely. Much was made of his influence on judging and his move for starting at 10 and dropping down according to what you see, rather than starting at a six or seven.

His book, Dressage Dreams 10, was fabulous and sadly a lot of what he pushed for has been lost in the past few years. Scores feel stuck on the average marks again.

Unless you are such a household name that receiving an eight or more seems a sure thing, it feels like the judges have been bullied out of risking really high marks. It may be that, with so much social media criticism and the fear of getting it wrong when everything is online for immediate scrutiny, it is difficult to stick one’s neck out.

“It feels like the judges have been bullied out of risking really high marks”

Unlike judges, keyboard warriors have the beauty of hindsight and can play back videos. Sometimes the judge that is out of line with the others is the one in the right, but was the only one that dared to err away from the six to 7.5 buttons.

I felt that if my mistake-free test on a nice horse is only just scraping the lower end of the 70s, it must be depressing for many others, who also had good tests but were shy of 70%. We need to take a leaf out of Stephen’s book, because we have lots of strong combinations, so how can so few tests then be getting good scores?

I would love to go back to fives and less for real mistakes but eight or more for deserving brilliance.

I felt the comments on my sheets were constructive and positive, but higher marks to match would be lovely for riders, owners and supporters, and so that when other nations look at our results, we are not selling ourselves short.

● What outside circumstances have derailed your competition performance? Let us know your thoughts at hhletters@futurenet.com, including your name, nearest town and county, for the chance to have your thoughts published in a future issue of Horse & Hound magazine

item.title: ‘The greatest dressage drama to be seen in Britain’: the 1996 Horse of the Year Show dressage freestyle that descended into fiasco
item.dc:content:
Heiner Schiergen shook his head.

His freestyle music had barely started when the German rider, last to go, signalled that something was wrong.

“When the 27-year-old rider entered the arena and gave the signal for his music to start, it commenced at the canter section,” wrote Richard Davison, who was riding in the class and covered the drama in his H&H column at the time.

It was the Sunday of the Horse of the Year Show (HOYS) at Wembley, and the freestyle finale of the Volvo dressage World Cup qualifier. Carole Mortimer’s H&H report at the time called what followed “the greatest dressage drama to be seen in Britain”.

Heiner wasn’t there to make up the numbers. He was riding the nine-year-old Hanoverian gelding Without A Doubt, and the pair had become firm crowd favourites after taking second place in the earlier grand prix – which then, as now, acted as a qualifier for the deciding freestyle.

“Amid scenes of great confusion, Heiner was left standing in the arena as chairman of the judges Eric Lette ran over to the technicians to be told that the first three minutes’ music were missing,” Richard wrote.

A race against the clock

The judges put the clock on and gave Heiner two minutes to fix the problem. Fellow German rider Frank Lamontagne, wrote Richard, “sprinted back to the horsebox for a spare tape.”

An H&H news report continued: “There was an agonising wait before his compatriot Frank Lamontagne came running into the arena with a duplicate tape.”

Frank’s return turned what was really a fairly minor mishap (what dressage rider hasn’t had trouble with their music, or doesn’t know one who has?) into something much more fun: a fiasco.

For a proper fiasco you need two things. High stakes – check. And a complete upending of the normal social order.

As Frank ran back into the arena clutching the spare tape – imagine that happening at the London International Horse Show where the World Cup qualifier is held today – that happened.

A crowd from a sport with a reputation for polite applause cheered him in like a returning hero. They were firmly on Heiner’s side, and they weren’t shy about showing it.

Frank, Richard recalled, was “greeted by cheers befitting the bearer of the Olympic flame”, and Heiner then “performed a good, lively test”.

Carole wrote: “He finished to immense applause and cheers from the enthusiastic supporters who were convinced his test could have won."

But that was only the first act of the fiasco – as the crowd began to settle, no score was forthcoming. Instead, it was belatedly announced that despite being allowed to perform his test, Heiner had been disqualified.

“The news was greeted with an even more vocal audience booing, jeering and stomping their feet,” Carole wrote. “A reaction more reminiscent of continental counterparts.”

The H&H news report described how “booing and foot-stamping turned to cheers as the rider entered the arena to debate the issue with chairman of the FEI dressage committee Eric Lette and Joep Bartels, the Volvo World Cup Dressage director” (pictured above). The uproar, it added, lasted “a full four minutes, continuing as organisers struggled to stick to a programme of presentations.”

The result got lost in it all. "The somewhat overshadowed victory belonged to Canadian Penny Rockx and 16-year-old Winsome,” Carole wrote, with our own Richard second on Askari.

The explanation

Despite the chaotic scenes, Eric Lette’s reasoning afterwards was quite straightforward. "After the bell has sounded, the rider has one minute to enter the arena," he said. “We gave him two minutes, but the final wait was nearer eight. The tape is the responsibility of the rider, and I must be fair to all the riders.”

In other words, Heiner had overshot the time allowed to start his test by some distance.

Richard said in his column that, as Eric explained at the press conference later, the decision had already been made before Heiner rode.

“As seven or eight minutes had elapsed before Heiner’s music began,” he said, “he was only allowed to ride on the understanding that the incident would go before the independent appeals committee. In the end, he decided not to appeal, no score was given and the disqualification stood.”

Heiner, for his part, saw it rather differently. “I think it would have been better to have been disqualified rather than letting me ride the whole test,” he said.

“A lot of time was wasted as I did not realise what the problem was. It was stressful waiting, but once I started riding my nerves disappeared, although I felt the horse had gone over.”

What happened to the tape?

Nobody could say. It was revealed afterwards that “somehow, part of the music programme had been blanked out.”

The show’s technicians insisted “the professionally-produced tape could not be tampered with,” but Lamontagne “claimed to have checked the tape three times before handing it to the technicians.”

Richard wrote: “Inevitably, rumours of sabotage circulated the arena. It was unpleasant for the technicians, and produced a most unsatisfactory end to what was otherwise an excellent competition.”

Richard’s verdict was that it was a “mix-up just waiting to happen”. Heiner and Without A Doubt were “the victims on this occasion”, he said, but “it could have happened to anyone at any show”.

item.dc:creator: Oscar Williams
item.dc:description: <p>Oscar joined <em>Horse & Hound</em> in October 2023 and is the magazine’s dressage editor and sports manager, overseeing coverage of equestrian sport.</p><p>Raised in Lancashire, Oscar started riding aged 12 and quickly became hooked. A keen member of the Lancaster & District branch of the Pony Club, he learnt to ride on a succession of hand-me-down ponies before persuading his parents to buy him his own horse – a wholly unsuitable but much-loved Welsh section C.</p><p>Oscar went on to study equine science at Myerscough College and, after deciding jumping wasn’t his strong suit, turned to dressage. Inspired by the London 2012 Olympics, he later spent four years working for leading trainer Emile Faurie. During that time, he competed at the 2015 National Dressage Championships and travelled with the yard to CDIs at Aachen, Vidauban, Saumur and Achleiten.</p><p>He also holds a master’s degree in Literature from York St John University (2021), combining his equestrian background with a passion for writing about the sport.</p><p>He regularly reports on elite dressage, breeding and welfare issues, as well as the science and policy shaping modern equestrian sport.</p><p>Oscar now lives in Cumbria with his two boisterous spaniels, Miffy and Dougal, and is interested in making equestrian sport more inclusive and accessible.</p>

item.title: ‘I always seem to end up with massive horses’: over 18hh eight-year-old won over all three judges to take the HOYS Future Elite dressage title
item.dc:content:
Laura Tomlinson won the Dressage Future Elite Championship at the Horse of the Year Show (HOYS) for the second time in three years on Thursday evening, this time with eight-year-old gelding Ostmarks Digal (Grand Galaxy x De Noir).

The Olympic gold medallist, who took the title in 2024 on the homebred Forest Hill, scored 77.79% for her inter I freestyle in the Andrews Bowen International Arena. All three judges placed the pair first, and they finished almost two percentage points clear of Gareth Hughes and Morricone III (75.92%), with Dannie Morgan and Fever Tree third (73.58%).

“I’m feeling quite excited that I’ve got something quite special under the saddle, and hopefully something really impressive for the future,” Laura said.

“I always seem to end up with massive horses! He is well over 18 hands, but he is very elegant with it and he is lovely to ride.”

Laura has had the gelding since December, when he arrived from the same German yard as her former top ride Rose Of Bavaria, who retired in 2024.

In eight outings since, he has not finished outside the top two and has won all but two tests. At the LeMieux National Dressage Championships last month, he won two titles, the Fairfax Saddles PSG gold (71.79%) and the D&H gold inter I (71.97%).

But it hasn’t always been plain sailing. “The first couple of times I rode him at a show, I wasn’t overly impressed – he was quite challenging to get on,” Laura told H&H last month. “But the more we get to know him, the easier he is.

“For me, this is a really great milestone for him. There is lots more work to be done, obviously, but it is nice already at this stage to feel like it is all there.”

Launched in 2013, the Dressage Future Elite Championship brings together Britain’s leading eight- to 10-year-old horses in an inter I freestyle. Previous winners include championship medallists Hawtins Delicato, Mount St John Freestyle, Imhotep and, of course, Jagerbomb, who won the title in 2022.

“It is a brilliant way to prepare them because you don’t get many atmospheres like this at the lower level when they are a bit younger to prepare them for what is to come in the future,” Laura said.

“So it is a great way to give these horses an opportunity like that, and I absolutely couldn’t be happier with how he handled it all.”

Dressage Future Elite Championship, HOYS 2026 – full results

  1. Laura Tomlinson and Ostmarks Digal – 77.79%
  2. Gareth Hughes and Morricone III – 75.92%
  3. Dannie Morgan and Fever Tree – 73.58%
  4. Matt Frost and Lenika – 72.83%
  5. Michael George Eilberg and EDH Saubermond – 72.17%
  6. Alexander Harrison and Ventura – 71.79%
  7. Demi Howard-Cartwright and Newton Astro Nascente – 69.83%
  8. Jody Haswell and Valentinio – 68.21%

Judges: Nick Burton (H), Clive Halsall (C), Andrea Smith (M)

  • To stay up to date with the latest news and reports throughout the Horse of the Year Show subscribe to the Horse & Hound website and enjoy our HOYS live news service throughout the show

item.title: 16 fantastic partnerships who enjoyed success at the final Riding Clubs championships of the season
item.dc:content:
Aston-le-Walls hosted the British Riding Clubs Howden Combined Championships (26–27 September).

There were 14 classes for Riding Club members – with scores counting for both individual and team results. These included a mix of combined training (dressage and showjumping), and combined challenge (showjumping and cross-country), over heights from 60cm–100cm.

Darc Legend’s competitive career came to an end in the best way when he was crowned overall champion in the open combined training with Joanne Watts.

The 18-year-old home-bred gelding has represented Carleton RC at numerous British Riding Clubs championships over the past 11 years and has multiple national titles to his name – including this one in 2022.

“He’s been an amazing stalwart and has never let us down,” said Joanne.

“He felt great today, and I was really pleased to finish on our dressage score. We’ve had some of our most enjoyable days at riding club events and to finish on a win is special.”

“He’s been an amazing stalwart and has never let us down”

Joanne Watts on her champion home-bred Darc Legend

Winners from the Riding Clubs Combined Championships

“She was weak when I got her and couldn’t canter more than three strides – but now she turns her hand to anything”

Sally Alsop on Crocus

“He’s only been cross-country four times, but he loves it”

Chloe Lewis on Mackanei

“They’re a team of young horses so we weren’t sure what would happen but they all held it together well”

Field House RC team manager Helen Berry

“I had two horses in this class which really helped as I was able to get a feel for the time on my first one”

edmund finlan

item.dc:creator: Martha Terry
item.dc:description: <p>An MA graduate in French and Italian from <a href="https://www.undergraduate.study.cam.ac.uk/courses/modern-medieval-languages-ba-hons" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">Cambridge University</a>, Martha initially started in the world of racing journalism on the bottom rungs of the <a href="https://www.racingpost.com/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>Racing Post</em></a>. She joined <em>H&H</em> as magazine assistant back in 2003, moving on to become eventing editor. She has worn many hats within the magazine since then, where she is now features editor.</p><p>In a reporting guise, Martha has been on the ground in Paris for the <a href="https://www.horseandhound.co.uk/paris-olympics-2024" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">2024 Olympics</a>, as well as multiple European Championships in both <a href="https://www.horseandhound.co.uk/blenheim-eventing-europeans" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">eventing</a> and <a href="https://www.horseandhound.co.uk/european-dressage-championships#:~:text=This%20year's%20European%20Dressage%20Championships,prix%20special%20and%20the%20freestyle." target="_blank" rel="nofollow">dressage</a>. Reporting has also taken her to Doha, the World Cup Finals in Riyadh, World Equestrian Festival in Aachen, Pau CCI5*, the young horse eventing world championships in <a href="https://www.horseandhound.co.uk/tag/le-lion-dangers" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">Le Lion d’Angers</a>, as well as closer to home at <a href="https://www.horseandhound.co.uk/burghley-horse-trials" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">Burghley</a>, <a href="https://www.horseandhound.co.uk/badminton-horse-trials" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">Badminton</a> and more local events at both grassroots and international level.</p><p>Martha has also written features on equestrian and rural matters for publications such as <a href="https://www.countrylife.co.uk/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>Country Life</em></a><em>, </em><a href="https://www.thefield.co.uk/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>The Field</em></a><em>, </em><a href="https://www.thetimes.com/?gclsrc=aw.ds&amp;&amp;utm_source=google&amp;utm_campaign=1463632778&amp;adgroupid=56048139559&amp;utm_medium=cpc&amp;utm_content=719979788324&amp;utm_term=thetimes%20com&amp;gad_source=1&amp;gad_campaignid=1463632778&amp;gbraid=0AAAAADiwoSDHBeWzU5_LOtXCF_HvthA0u&amp;gclid=CjwKCAjwq9rFBhAIEiwAGVAZP_YFIluhUTLlalBzcOhU8WYiJh8_DsSgIZadDNhX2HQSfw-Zn8RmuRoCx6MQAvD_BwE" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>The Times</em></a><em>, </em><a href="https://www.spectator.co.uk/writer/martha-terry/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>The Spectator</em></a><em>, </em><a href="https://www.polotimes.co.uk/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>Polo Times</em></a> and <a href="https://www.telegraph.co.uk/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>The Telegraph</em></a>, and has covered everything from an exclusive on The Queen’s favourite horses and the cloning of Tamarillo to interviewing the iconic Jilly Cooper.</p><p>Martha is regularly called on to contribute to TV programmes on equestrian royalty, such as ITN’s <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt11892448/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>All The Queen’s Horses</em></a> and a 2025 Channel 5 documentary on <a href="https://www.channel5.com/show/princess-anne-a-quite-remarkable-royal" target="_blank" rel="nofollow"><em>Princess Anne, A Quite Remarkable Royal</em></a>.</p><p>Born and raised in Suffolk, Martha has ridden since she was eight, initially with the Essex & Suffolk branch of the Pony Club and going on to event up to intermediate level though with very little success, despite having lessons with the great Ruth McMullen. Martha has bred two event horses by Cevin Z from her own horse of a lifetime, Fizz, one of which is now eventing at CCI4* with Alice Hallows.</p><p>Martha is currently enjoying producing a seven-year-old ex-racehorse, Mac, who she believes might need someone better and braver than her to do him justice in eventing. She enjoys jumping, hacking and fitness work.</p><p>Martha is also besotted with dogs – with a huge soft spot for springer spaniels – though with no competitive ambitions in this sphere whatsoever. After growing up with assorted liver and white springers, she had two rescue dogs for 14 years, one a street dog from Gambia who was abandoned at three weeks old. Now, her constant companion, whether by her feet at her desk or walking cross-country courses, is Fidget, an extremely energetic and habitually muddy black and white springer.</p><p>Martha also writes for expert advice guide <a href="https://www.petsradar.com/author/martha-terry" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">PetsRadar</a>, and was editor for Petplan Equine’s magazine <em>Paces</em> for seven years.</p>

item.title: ‘We’re very, very excited’: double world medallist and husband expecting first child
item.dc:content:
Para dressage double world medallist Jemima Green and her husband Ed Chapman are expecting their first child.

“Baby Chapman” is due via surrogate in March 2027, and Jemima told H&H she and Ed are “very excited”.

“It’s quite daunting because it’s something we’ve never done, but we’re so ready for it,” she said.

“We’re not going to find out the sex, as much as Ed would love to know. I think it’s one of the biggest surprises you can get.”

Jemima said she and Ed started looking into the surrogacy process almost four years ago; it has been a long journey. The couple underwent IVF and the embryo was transferred to a surrogate mother.

“We had to go down the surrogacy route because of the amount of abdominal damage I had and I’m just now allowed to carry,” said Jemima.

“It’s been a whole new world going through the process and finding out all the legal information. Even though the baby is 100% genetically ours, there’s still so many hurdles you have to go through.

“There’s been every kind of emotion, and just getting to terms with having to have a family in a different way, but it’s amazing that we’ve got the opportunity to do it. Ed’s been so supportive and understood from day one.”

Jemima and Ed have been at all the pre-natal appointments and scans.

“We’ve very lucky that we have a great relationship with our surrogate and we’re able to go to the scans. It’s also being mindful of hospital surrogacy rules as they’re not all the same about how many people can attend,” said Jemima.

“Last week was the first time we heard the heartbeat, so that’s a huge milestone. It would’t be the same getting it over a video, so we’re very lucky hospitals have been very accommodating of our process.”

Jemima has had a 2026 to remember, having won individual bronze and silver with Fantabulous at the World Championships in Aachen in August.

“Last year the Europeans was our first championship and I just felt so lucky to be there. It’s not that I didn’t deserve the spot, but this year I was really thinking: ‘We have campaigned well, we really deserve our place’,” she said.

“We got the silver in the freestyle and a personal best of 80%. It was bit of a whirlwind as we got home on the Monday and had the 12-week scan on the Wednesday.”

Jemima plans to keep competing with “Fanta” once Baby Chapman arrives.

“I thought about it, and as I’m not having to physically recover, I’m going to keep riding and campaigning,” she said.

“It’s going to be full-on, but we’re very lucky Ed’s mum is close by. Even if I do need to drop down to riding less days, my coach Georgie [Nicholls] helps me with Fanta and so he’ll be kept running exactly like normal. I like being organised and I love a list, so planning ahead is absolutely something I’m looking forward to doing. We’re very, very excited.”

She moved up to senior news writer in January 2022. During her time at <em>H&H</em> she has reported on a broad range of topics across the equestrian industry including welfare issues, veterinary studies, FEI Tribunal hearings, rider safety, and road safety campaigns. In 2019 she attended the national Strangles Symposium and the Scottish welfare conference.</p><p>Becky was part of the home remote reporting team for the Tokyo and Paris Olympic Games as well as multiple European Championships. She has reported in person from Morris Equestrian, the Royal Highland Show, Blair Castle, Scone Palace and Luhmühlen. She is attending the 2025 European Para Dressage Championships as Horse & Hound’s on-site reporter.</p><p>Based in north Scotland, Becky learnt to ride at the age of five. She got the showjumping bug with her 13.2hh older pony Phoenix, who used to particularly enjoy a chase-me-Charlie. After losing two horses in 2015 to illness and injury, Becky is now producing two Irish mares, Ruby and Chloe, and hopes to get back in the showjumping ring in the future. She also has two miniature Shetland sisters, Mootie and Poppet, who keep her on her toes.</p>

item.content:encoded:
Para dressage double world medallist Jemima Green and her husband Ed Chapman are expecting their first child.

“Baby Chapman” is due via surrogate in March 2027, and Jemima told H&H she and Ed are “very excited”.

“It’s quite daunting because it’s something we’ve never done, but we’re so ready for it,” she said.

“We’re not going to find out the sex, as much as Ed would love to know. I think it’s one of the biggest surprises you can get.”

Jemima said she and Ed started looking into the surrogacy process almost four years ago; it has been a long journey. The couple underwent IVF and the embryo was transferred to a surrogate mother.

“We had to go down the surrogacy route because of the amount of abdominal damage I had and I’m just now allowed to carry,” said Jemima.

“It’s been a whole new world going through the process and finding out all the legal information. Even though the baby is 100% genetically ours, there’s still so many hurdles you have to go through.

“There’s been every kind of emotion, and just getting to terms with having to have a family in a different way, but it’s amazing that we’ve got the opportunity to do it. Ed’s been so supportive and understood from day one.”

Jemima and Ed have been at all the pre-natal appointments and scans.

“We’ve very lucky that we have a great relationship with our surrogate and we’re able to go to the scans. It’s also being mindful of hospital surrogacy rules as they’re not all the same about how many people can attend,” said Jemima.

item.title: ‘I’ve never had so much fun’: Olympic dressage rider finishes runner-up on eventing debut
item.dc:content:
Olympic dressage rider Abi Lyle swapped her tailcoat for cross-country colours to finish runner-up on her British Eventing debut.

Abi and Becca McCreath’s eight-year-old gelding Nice Try II (Obi) were competing in the GoBE80 at Little Gatcombe on 19 September.

“I’ve been wanting to do an event for ages but life got in the way or events got cancelled, so I was happy that I finally got to do something before the season ends,” Abi told H&H.

“It was my proper debut and hopefully it will be the first of many!”

Abi and Obi led the first two phases, having posted a 24 dressage.

“Obi is such a little gentleman, and this was only his fourth or fifth event,” said Abi.

“He’s one of these really nice horses that will go on the bit and be really consistent. I was riding him round thinking, ‘Oh, I’d like a bit more of this or that’ but had to remind myself: ‘No, this is eventing dressage!’

“We showjumped clear and he was a really good boy. Becky keeps Obi at Aston-le-Walls so I’ve been having plenty of lessons with Nigel Taylor in preparation.”

Abi and Obi jumped clear across country, with four time-faults, to finish second.

“Before I set off the steward asked if I was Abi the dressage rider, and said: ‘Good for you, well done’ and I was like: ‘Hang on, I haven’t got round yet’,” said Abi.

“I had my plan, but I’m ashamed to say I was heaving and wheezing by fence seven! There’s probably no limit to how much sitting trot I could do – but my God I was exhausted going round a cross-country. I’ve never had so much fun but also want something to end at the same time.

“We did lose the win for time-penalties, but I loved every minute, and probably because I was so knackered I didn’t over-ride him. He was fantastic. I finished and thought ‘I need to do this again’.”

Abi enjoyed the eventing community spirit.

“Eventing is so cool, everyone’s friendly and helpful. When people are jumping their rounds they’re whooping and saying ‘Good boy’, it’s just so nice to see people enjoying their horses like that,” she said.

“Dressage is fun but you can’t really express it, but in eventing you see people being ‘Woo’ and I just thought that was class. In the lorry park we were chatting away to our neighbours, and it was all just really lovely.”

Abi hopes to borrow Obi for some more events next season, when he is not competing with his owner Becca. In the meantime she is producing five-year-old mare Pipsqueak – whose competition name is Anti-Hero, a nod to the Swifties – bred by Abi’s friend and yard owner Georgie Round. Abi and Pipsqueak are competing in their first hunter trials this weekend at West Wilts.

“She’s called Pipsqueak because she was really little when she was a baby, she’s a little cutie,” said Abi.

“She’s not got the decorum for a one-day event yet, but she’ll jump anything you put in front of her. We did a little training event at Aston and she didn’t look at anything, she just loves it. We’ll put the work in over winter and hopefully we’ll be set up and ready to go out at the start of next season.”

But dressage fans can rest assured, Abi isn’t hanging up her tailcoat. She is entered for the Kronenberg CDI in Belgium next month with her Olympic ride Giraldo, known at home as Arty.

“I’ll always be dressage,” she said. “Arty feels great so I thought ‘Let’s not spend the winter festering, let’s get out’ – and it’s supposed to be a really nice show.”

Abi is also adding another string to her bow, having this week started a part-time criminology and law degree through the Open University.

“I previously did university in something else but never finished, and it’s always weighed on my mind. Since the Paris Olympics, I thought, ‘I’ve done that, and now I want to get a bit of academia in there’,” said Abi.

“The course takes six years, so I’m going to just see where I’m at. I’m super interested in the criminal justice system and with my past experiences, I’d love to apply myself to help in more significant ways that I currently do, so I thought this would be a good place to start.

“It’s online study and I spend a lot of time flying and in airports when I’m away teaching, so I can make use of that time. My priority is still to keep going with the horses; I’ve got Arty and some of Fenella’s [Quinn] lovely horses that are exciting and I definitely want to do some internationals next year.”

item.title: ‘Alarmingly, the LA28 Olympics is only 19 shoeing cycles away,’ warns Anna Ross
item.dc:content:
The LeMieux National Dressage Championships have been and gone. Sometimes the grand prix field suffers after the major championships, when top contenders are resting their horses. This year, championship team riders filled the first three places, with one on a horse who had been to the worlds.

Alarmingly, we are less than two years from another Olympics, which is five minutes or 19 shoeing cycles in horse terms.

The talent behind the top three impressed. Olivia Oakeley returned to grand prix 10 years after her last horse competed at that level, proving that tenacity wins. That’s a reality check for riders expecting to sail directly on an upward trajectory to stardom after under-25 level.

The best nationals stories happen behind the scenes. Tig Abel secured her broken toe inside a dog poo bag to get her boots on and rode a successful championship, and wrote a hilarious Facebook blog. Sadie Smith’s horse returned a year after a terrible road accident to win the seven-year-old class and the tribute to Stephen Clarke was beautiful.

I agree with Richard Davison that implementing the code of points Stephen worked so hard on as a way of judging dressage would be a fitting legacy. A more transparent sport would truly honour a judge who made riders feel anything was possible – even on the bad days when it wasn’t.

London pleases the grinch in me

Just as British Dressage members start to feel the winter blues, all is not lost as we are in for a Christmas treat. The next major highlight is the London International and spectators are going to get more “bang for their buck” as this new concept will include a pilot class for seven-year-olds and upcoming grand prix horses as well as the World Cup.

Two days of top riders, upcoming star horses, fan zones and an opportunity to be up close with a glass of champagne or a nice cappuccino in the warm sounds like the stuff of dreams. Better than Christmas anyway – as the official “grinch” of our stables, I’ll swap it for a trip to the Excel any day.

Is this my new “secret weapon”?

I have a couple of horses ready for grand prix and eagle-eyed online observers noticed that I’ve been riding with one rein upside down, so the part going to the horse’s mouth comes from the top of the hand rather than the bottom, prompting Facebook experts to debate whether I’m using an advanced technique from the old masters.

I considered claiming it was my new secret weapon but actually, arthritis in my hand means I just can’t hold the rein conventionally. The horses haven’t noticed, which is reassuring but also slightly irritating having worked hard to keep my thumbs on top for 30 years.

A recent article suggested riders spend £5,000 competing on teams abroad. Those of us who have done it muttered, “and the rest”. Britain’s international calendar is therefore welcome and Hickstead’s return with the Nations Cup is a bonus. Let us hope other nations cross the Channel.

Perhaps composite teams could return, whereby if a smaller nation based here couldn’t field a team of four, riders from different nations could band together, which used to be good fun.

Returning to the competition arena

I’ve entered some competitions as it was sarcastically pointed out by our team that my last rosette was won by Barney, my spaniel, for third in waggiest tail at our local dog show. Barney won some warm prosecco and a packet of artichoke seeds.

To be fair, I have returned from internationals with less useful prizes.

An ashtray, a trophy resembling an Ann Summers window display and some socks are among the treasure trove. A fellow international rider told me she won a book that someone had clearly already read. Winning a grand prix in Spain earned me two leg wraps and you had to win the special to complete the set.

Every new grand prix horse feels like starting again, so I’ve polished up my bling, got a new tailcoat and I’m getting out there to have some fun.

● What’s the least useful prize you’ve won? Let us know your thoughts at hhletters@futurenet.com, including your name, nearest town and county, for the chance to have your thoughts published in a future issue of Horse & Hound magazine
