item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Horse & Hound’s live blog from the 2026 LeMieux National Dressage Championships. Our dressage editor Oscar Williams was on the ground at Somerford Park, bringing you results, highlights and reaction as they happened.

From prelim to grand prix, we followed the action across every arena and caught up with riders as the titles were decided. Refresh this page throughout the day for updates, quotes and clips.

  • How to watch the 2026 LeMieux National Dressage Championships
  • Live scores
September 10, 2026 – 6:31 AM

Thursday

Hello, it’s Oscar here at a blustery Somerford Park. Today’s championships include the Fairfax Saddles prix st georges (PSG) gold – featuring standout combinations like Gareth Hughes on up-and-coming star Morricone III and Laura Tomlinson on Ostmarks Digal – plus the HorseQuest elementary silver, the Stübben inter I gold and the Absolute Equestrian Collective prelim silver.

The Equissage para gold championship was on early and has already wrapped up – we’ll be bringing you reactions from the winners as we get it.

September 10, 2026 – 6:48 AM

Gareth Hughes has just ridden in the Fairfax Saddles PSG Gold, scoring 70.21% on Morricone III to go into provisional second behind Matt Frost and Lenika (70.53%).

The 10-year-old stallion looks a good prospect for the future – Gareth describes him as a “stunning-looking horse who is good in both collection and extended paces.”

It’s a mammoth class with 41 competitors and we’re only five in, so there’s still plenty of time for the leaderboard to change.

September 10, 2026 – 6:59 AM

Results are in from this morning’s Equissage para gold championships:

Sophie Wells rounded off a superb season with a one-two in grade V, winning on MSJ Gold Standard – the mare she rode to an emotional individual gold at last month’s World Championships in Aachen – ahead of her own second ride, Ontario HL.

In grade I, Mari Durward-Akhurst topped the class on Watermill Cruise, stepping into the breach left by the retirement of long-serving partner Athene Lindebjerg, who carried her to individual silver at Aachen.

Grade I

1st: Mari Durward-Akhurst – Watermill Cruise (71.67%)

2nd: Elan Williams – Nalique (71.18%)

3rd: Susanna Wade – Premier Royal Mint (69.72%)

Grade II

1st: Georgia Wilson – Koningin Rava LH (72.56%)

2nd: Vicky Earnshaw – Midline Rioja (65.72%)

3rd: Julie Payne – Divinity (65.39%)

Grade III

No entrants

Grade IV

1st: Laura Scott – CEI Summer Days (69.91%)

2nd: Sara Bates – Tango VII (69.1%)

3rd: Katie Radzik – Korsgårds Tempt-Hit (68.15%)

Grade V

1st: Sophie Wells – MSJ Gold Standard (71.54%)

2nd: Sophie Wells – Ontario HL (67.98%)

3rd: Loretta Joynson – Tresais Lancelot (63.11%)

September 10, 2026 – 7:19 AM

We have a new leader in the PSG gold – Laura Tomlinson and new ride Ostmarks Digal, who’ve pulled out an impressive 71.67% to lead.

They’d have been among the pre-competition favourites, but there’s plenty more still to come:

Dannie Morgan and Fever Tree (1.30pm, LeMieux Arena) – the up-and-coming horse Dannie has said Carl Hester told him was “the best horse in the country”

Ruby Hughes and Fire Kracka (1.54pm)

Amy Woodhead and MSJ Viva Donnebrog (2.02pm)

Michael Eilberg and EDH Nanouk (2.42pm)

September 10, 2026 – 7:56 AM

We’re into a break in the Fairfax Saddles PSG gold – here’s how the top five stand:

1st: Laura Tomlinson – Ostmarks Digal (71.79%)

2nd: Matt Frost – Lenika (70.53%)

3rd: Gareth Hughes – Morricone III (70.21%)

4th: Louise Gallavan-Gelder – Fabergé TF (69.21%)

5th: Kate Cowell – Samarkand (69.00%)

Next up when action resumes is Dannie Morgan on Fever Tree at 1.30pm.

September 10, 2026 – 8:02 AM

Over in the Vector Arena, Harriet Dixon and Dark Storm lead the Absolute Equestrian Collective prelim silver on 71% – a comfortable margin ahead of second-placed Jill Stevenson and Parthago HBF on 69.93%. There are 18 more to go in that class.

Now to the Kudos Arena, where Isabel White and Quatango have led for a while... no, wait – Amber Flynn and Fortuna BG have just overtaken them, scoring 70.67%! Just four riders to go in that one.

September 10, 2026 – 8:46 AM

Dannie Morgan and Fever Tree are into the arena, restarting the PSG gold.

The eight-year-old gelding flows through the early trot work with lots of suspension. Oh, that’s strange – his scores ranged from 4 to 8.5 on the first medium trot... I didn’t see a mistake.

The trot work was outstanding bar a slight mistake in the second volte, but they’re being hammered on the walk, unfortunately, with Fever Tree rushing the second walk half-pirouette. That’s expensive, because both the collected and extended walk are double-marked.

He flies through the canter work – again there’s some up-and-down judging – to score 66.94% for provisional eighth. That’s one of the big hitters falling by the wayside, and my prediction blown out of the water. But there’s plenty to come from Fever Tree, and Dannie shouldn’t be too disappointed.

The judging was a bit all over the place for this one. Here’s the breakdown, with the judges from abroad – including former Olympian Sven Rothenberger – marking it lower than the Brits:

E – Sue McMahon (GBR): 70.44% (ranked 5th)

H – Richard Baldwin (GBR): 67.21% (ranked 10th)

C – Nick Burton (GBR): 69.85% (ranked 4th)

M – Sven Rothenberger (NED): 64.71% (ranked 12th)

B – Øivind Instefjord Oedemotland (NOR): 62.50% (ranked 13th)

September 10, 2026 – 9:06 AM

Fresh from her grade I gold on new ride Watermill Cruise, Mari Durward-Akhurst has been telling us more about the horse who's stepping up after the retirement of long-time partner Athene Lindebjerg.

“It’s only our third major show together, so we’re still a bit of a new partnership, but I was really pleased with it,” Mari said. “The connection was better – we just need a bit more forwardness into it, but it’s all coming together. He was amazing, such a good boy in a bigger atmosphere. He just went in and did his job.”

The gelding switched from eventing, and Mari says the physical transformation has taken time: “His walk has got better and better – he’s had to change the muscles from eventing to dressage. He‘s much stronger now; people don’t recognise him, he looks very different to when we got him. It’s taken about a year.

“He’s done loads of carrot stretches, and he’s got his physio routine, same as I’ve got mine – then it’s just the eight-metre circles, he’s over 17hh so they’re quite small for a big horse.”

Looking ahead, the target is clear: “Obviously the aim is the LA Paralympics, and maybe the Europeans next summer. He’s got ginormous shoes to fill after Athene, but he seems to have the temperament, which I think is really important, and he’s got the walk, so it’s just knitting it all together.”

September 10, 2026 – 9:18 AM

We’ve had a couple more of the favourites go in the PSG gold.

Ruby Hughes and Fire Kracka – who’s not long returned after a suspensory injury suffered in June last year – score 70.12% to slot in just behind her dad, Gareth Hughes on Morricone III (70.21%).

The pair had a mistake in the flying change after the second canter half-pirouette, with the nine-year-old stallion looking late behind from where I sit at H. This horse is known for his extended walk, and it’s outstanding here again, scoring 8s and 8.5s – such a brilliant banker for an up-and-coming horse, seeing as it’s double-marked.

Then it’s Amy Woodhead and MSJ Viva Donnebrog, who are flying through the early trot work – this mare is such an athlete, scoring a 9 for the medium trot. But mistakes in the walk half-pirouette and changes peg them back to 69.24%.

The walk half-pirouettes are proving a challenge for a few combinations out there.

September 10, 2026 – 9:21 AM

The final results are now in from the HorseQuest elementary silver... and it’s Amber Flynn and Fortuna BG who’ve held on to win on 70.67%.

We’ll try to catch up with Amber after her prizegiving at 2.50pm.

September 10, 2026 – 9:26 AM

A picture from earlier in the day of Sophie Wells aboard grade V gold winner MSJ Gold Standard – the mare on whom she won World Championship gold in Aachen last month.

With owner Emma Blundell planning to sell the 10-year-old after this season, today’s win could be one of the pair’s last together.

September 10, 2026 – 9:32 AM

We’ve had a few more go in the PSG gold, but Laura Tomlinson and Ostmarks Digal (71.79%) remain in the lead.

It’s worth remembering that even with a few mistakes, riders will be keen to get a good score on the board – there’s still plenty to play for. The top 15 move forward to tomorrow’s freestyle (11 September), and the overall Fairfax Saddles PSG supreme champion is decided on the combination of today’s score and that freestyle result.

September 10, 2026 – 9:40 AM

Laura Scott, who won grade IV gold earlier today on CEI Summer Days (69.91%) – a repeat of last year’s win in this class – gave us the lowdown on the ride.

On the test itself: “He was really good – he always loves coming into a big arena, it kind of sets him alight a bit. He were really consistent the whole way through, and he tried really hard for me every inch of the way.”

On the work still to come: “He’s still a bit of a work in progress – he’s building the strength for more collection, but you start to see glimmers of it in his tests. When we can deliver at home what we deliver in a test, he’ll go up a gear again.”

On her ambitions for the gelding: “I’d love to go abroad to an international with him next year, and I’d love to get selected for a team one day – that’s the main goal.

“We’ve obviously got to improve a bit more to get there, but I think he’s got the ability. I’ve just got to keep up with him.”

September 10, 2026 – 9:45 AM

It’s all happening now – next door to the main arena, in the Kudos Arena, we have the Stübben inter II underway, with 24 starters. The weather looks ominous – a few of the later combinations might get a bit wet. We never luck out on the weather here, do we?

Emma Jablonski currently leads on Higgens Van De Uilenhoek, scoring 67.91%.

September 10, 2026 – 9:57 AM

A couple more combinations who you’d expect to be right up there have gone in the PSG gold – but Laura Tomlinson and Ostmarks Digal remain in the lead (71.79%).

Michael Eilberg and EDH Nanouk – a Premier League winner this season – score 68.82%, while Fiona Bigwood and Newton Sylvanite score 69.06%.

Just four combinations have exceeded 70% so far – the judges are proving hard to please today.

September 10, 2026 – 10:21 AM

I caught up with Amber Flynn, who grooms for Irish team rider Jess Dunn – who competed at the World Championships in Aachen – at White Hill Stud, and has just won the HorseQuest elementary silver on Fortuna BG:

“I was thrilled with the whole test, to be honest. My trot work was really strong, and my canter work is always the bit I’m a bit nervous about: the counter-canter and the simple changes. I usually get one or the other, but both felt really solid today, and she felt like she wanted to show off a little bit.

“She won the Area Festival Championships freestyle-to-music novice class last year, but this is our first national championship title.

“I’ve not had loads of prep for this, really, because I was in Aachen with Jess. But it didn’t seem to work against me, so maybe less prep is better for me. Maybe then I can’t overthink it.

“I was a little bit distracted at the beginning of the test because she had a fly on her neck, and she started shaking her head in the first two movements to get it off.

“I thought, I hope this fly isn’t going to stay there the whole test. But luckily, it buggered off, and after that I felt like I could concentrate a bit more. But at first I was a bit worried she was going to do it the whole way round!”

September 10, 2026 – 10:30 AM

We have a new leader in the Stübben inter I: Tom Goode and Margot have just gone into the lead, scoring 70.77%.

Ruby Hughes – on her second ride of the day, Farrell, Abi Lyle’s former European Championship ride – is next in.

September 10, 2026 – 10:39 AM

Oh, that’s close – but not quite close enough. Ruby scores 70.44% to slot in just 0.22% behind Tom and Margot.

September 10, 2026 – 10:49 AM

Back to the PSG gold in the main arena, where it’s really starting to rain now, as Gracie Catling and her exciting Friesian mare Fraithwens Wytske Fan Ter Lune score 64.65% – with unfortunate mistakes in the changes.

22-year-old Gracie is one of the most talked-about young riders in British dressage right now. She swept three of four small tour titles at this year’s Winter Championships and produces all her horses herself at the family yard in Oxfordshire – no coach, no ready-made warmbloods.

Of Wytske, she’s previously told us: “She’s the only horse that has ever taken my breath away – we call her a dragon, but she’s a bit like a swan, she’s got this look on her face that she knows she’s better than everyone else.”

September 10, 2026 – 10:52 AM

And now over to the Vector Arena – I’m getting whiplash – where we have a winner in the Absolute Equestrian Collective prelim silver. Mary Pearson and Bella Vista have taken it on 71.07%, a fraction up on early leaders Harriet Dixon and Dark Storm, who finish second on 71%.

September 10, 2026 – 11:18 AM

Olivia Oakley is the last to go before the final break in the Fairfax Saddles PSG gold. In a fetching bright blue tailcoat she scores 65.71% on Nulli Secundus 11 to go into provisional 27th. Here’s the current top five, and Laura remains out in front:

1st: Laura Tomlinson – Ostmarks Digal (71.79%)

2nd: Matt Frost – Lenika (70.53%)

3rd: Gareth Hughes – Morricone III (70.21%)

4th: Ruby Hughes – Fire Kracka (70.12%)

5th: Amy Woodhead – MSJ Viva Donnebrog (69.24%)

September 10, 2026 – 11:35 AM

We have a new leader in the Stübben inter II gold – Michael Eilberg and MSJ Dante VX, runners-up in this class two years ago, score 72.56% to storm into the lead.

September 10, 2026 – 11:43 AM

I think Michael has this... Just three left to go in this class: Becky Edwards and Dita Von Teese, Rowan Bryson and Izonik and Millie Gover and Kamil.

September 10, 2026 – 12:03 PM

Amber Flynn and Fortuna BG celebrate winning the HorseQuest elementary silver at the 2026 LeMieux National Dressage Championships.

“I definitely wasn’t expecting to win. It’s a massive class, and I know she’s quite consistent in scores and can pull off a really nice test, but I think I just have to have a bit more confidence riding in a competition test.”

September 10, 2026 – 12:13 PM

The Stübben inter II gold is done and dusted, with Michael Eilberg and MSJ Dante VX taking the win:

1st: Michael Eilberg – MSJ Dante VX (72.56%)

2nd: Tom Goode – Margot (70.77%)

3rd: Ruby Hughes – Farrell (70.44%)

4th: Lucy Amy – Rudy (69.91%)

5th: Anders Dahl – Ellely’s Focus (68.09%)

September 10, 2026 – 12:23 PM

Mary Pearson and coloured mare Bella Vista celebrate winning the Absolute Equestrian Collective prelim silver at the 2026 LeMieux National Dressage Championships.

September 10, 2026 – 12:24 PM

Here’s the last three to go in the PSG gold – can anyone catch Laura? Ben Martin and Jacko B (5.26), Sara-Jane Lanning and Hawtins Lirica (5.34) and Eilidh Grant and Lebora (5.42) still have their chance.

September 10, 2026 – 12:52 PM

They gave it their best shot – but none of Ben, Sara-Jane or Eilidh could catch winners Laura Tomlinson and Ostmarks Digal who win the Fairfax Saddles PSG gold national title.

Ben and Jacko B scored 67%, Sara-Jane and Hawtins Lirica 68.82% to finish 10th and Eilidh Grant a disappointing 61.65%.
Here are the top 15 who’ve qualified for tomorrow’s Fairfax Saddles PSG freestyle (11 September):

  1. Laura Tomlinson – Ostmarks Digal (71.79%)
  2. Matt Frost – Lenika (70.53%)
  3. Gareth Hughes – Morricone III (70.21%)
  4. Ruby Hughes – Fire Kracka (70.12%)
  5. Bryony Goodwin – Krack DE (69.53%)
  6. Amy Woodhead – MSJ Viva Donnebrog (69.24%)
  7. Louise Gallavan-Gelder – Fabergé TF (69.21%)
  8. Fiona Bigwood – Newton Sylvanite (69.06%)
  9. Kate Cowell – Samarkand (69.00%)
  10. Michael Eilberg – EDH Nanouk (68.82%)
  11. Sara-Jane Lanning – Hawtins Lirica (68.82%)
  12. Amy Woodhead – Extra II (68.68%)
  13. Alexander Harrison – Ventura (68.59%)
  14. Robert Barker – Borlandeaus (68.27%)
  15. Claire Abel – GF Sezuki (67.97%)
September 10, 2026 – 12:53 PM

Stick with us – we’ll have all the reaction from PSG winner Laura Tomlinson and inter II winner Michael Eilberg to follow..

September 10, 2026 – 1:17 PM

Michael Eilberg on inter II gold winner MSJ Dante VX:

“This is a class that’s eluded me for a long time. I’ve had some close calls with him, Half Moon Delphi and with other horses too – I’ve always ended up messing up this class somehow. I’m so chuffed because he’s very special to me, and he's the one who got it for me.

“He just did a very solid test. We’ve been working on his confidence in the piaffe, and that was better today. He walked extremely well, showed expression where it was needed, and calmness where it was needed too.

“We’ve had him up at this level a couple of years now, and he’s starting to feel really comfortable – the canter feels really easy for him, everything feels established for grand prix. It’s just the piaffe, because he’s a bit sensitive – he still needs time to mature there.”

September 10, 2026 – 1:23 PM

Laura Tomlinson on PSG winner Ostmarks Digal:

“I was really happy. He obviously hasn’t competed since Hartpury [July], so it’s been a while – but we’ve done our homework over the summer and that was definitely his best test yet.

“There was a moment in the first half-pass where he could have got a little spicy, but he made a very grown-up decision and stayed with me.

“He’s by Grand Galaxy – I’ve had him since last December. He came from the same yard that had Rose of Bavaria beforehand.

“He’s quirky, but once he knows who his people are, he trusts you. The first couple of times I rode him at a show, I wasn’t overly impressed; he was quite challenging to get on and even yesterday he was a bit fidgety – but today he was already so much better.

“I think once he knows his people, he trusts you, and it gets easier. He’s very talented, and I think he’ll be a really fun horse to bring up the levels.”

Laura also confirmed the gelding won’t contest tomorrow’s freestyle: “He’s going to do the inter I tomorrow instead – that’s enough for him. I don’t want to be greedy. He’s only eight – I don’t want him to do three tests in a row.”

September 10, 2026 – 1:34 PM

The two walk half-pirouettes were a real challenge for several combinations in the PSG, but Laura and Ostmarks Digal averaged a class high 7.5 across the pair.

“I’ve had them drummed into me heavily since I was a pony rider,” Laura said. “I quite like them, because they trip a lot of people up, so it’s a good one to show off.

“He’s a nice active horse with a very good collected walk, so you don’t have to adjust too much going into the pirouette – you can come in smoother. I think a lot of people push too much from the quarters and the horse gets stuck coming round – for me, it’s all about bringing the shoulder first.”

September 10, 2026 – 1:45 PM

Michael Eilberg on inter II gold winner MSJ Dante VX: “He’s done me a great service with this class, because this is a class that’s eluded me for a long time.

“I’ve had some close calls with him, and I think he’s been in the mix a couple of times with other horses too, but I’ve always ended up messing up this class somehow.”

September 10, 2026 – 1:55 PM

Laura Tomlinson went early in the order in the PSG gold, back when the class kicked off at 11.04am – and with 41 combinations to get through, it made for a very long wait to find out where she stood:

“It’s not a massive score – I had a couple of higher scores in there, but two not-so-high ones too. I think everyone had me in first except for one. It was such a long day I’d actually switched off from it a bit. I was asleep for an hour just before – passed out in my lorry – and woke up to find out I’d won, which was nice.”

September 10, 2026 – 2:08 PM

It’s been a packed first day at Somerford Park – here’s how the titles fell:

Equissage Gold Para Dressage Championships

Grade I: Mari Durward-Akhurst – Watermill Cruise (71.67%)

Grade II: Georgia Wilson – Koningin Rava LH (72.56%)

Grade III: no entrants

Grade IV: Laura Scott – CEI Summer Days (69.91%), retaining her title from last year

Grade V: Sophie Wells – MSJ Gold Standard (71.54%), a one-two ahead of her own Ontario HL

Fairfax Saddles PSG gold: Laura Tomlinson and new ride Ostmarks Digal lead on 71.79%.

Absolute Equestrian Collective prelim silver: Mary Pearson and Bella Vista (71.07%), edging out early leader Harriet Dixon and Dark Storm (71.00%).

HorseQuest elementary silver: Amber Flynn and Fortuna BG, known at home as Cookie (70.67%) – fresh off grooming duty for Jess Dunn at the World Championships in Aachen.

Stübben inter II gold: Michael Eilberg and MSJ Dante VX (72.56%), overtaking early leader Tom Goode and Margot (70.77%) – a class that’s eluded Michael for years, finally in the bag.

What’s coming up on day two

Friday brings 145 starts across three arenas – here’s the pick of it:

LeMieux Arena: the D&H gold inter I championship gets going at 8.05am, before the big one – the Fairfax Saddles PSG freestyle gold championship at 3.20pm, where the overall supreme champion will be decided. With Laura Tomlinson sitting the freestyle out on Ostmarks Digal, that title race is wide open.

Fiona Bigwood topped the board in the KBIS young horse test for four-year-olds this morning on BPS Supreme Bella (by Sezuan). The mare is the latest in a striking three-generation damline Fiona has bred and produced herself.

Granddam Atterupgaards Orthilia was Fiona’s ride on the silver-medal-winning British teams at the 2015 Europeans and 2016 Olympics. Dam Donna Bella was Fiona’s World Championship ride in Aachen. A remarkable turnaround for River Rise Onassis

Sadie Smith has won the KBIS young horse test for seven-year-olds on River Rise Onassis, scoring 81.17% for owner Sue Garrard – but it's the horse's journey back to this arena that makes the result so special.

Almost exactly a year ago, River Rise Onassis was travelling home from these same championships, having finished third in last year”s six-year-old final, when her horsebox was hit from behind on the M6 in atrocious weather and overturned across all three lanes.

Sue Garrard, driving, escaped with her but was left dangling in the horse area for three hours, trying to keep Sassy calm amid sharp metal and glass while they waited for a vet to arrive and sedate her. “I thought she was dead,” Sue said at the time.

A year on, River Rise Onassis is back at Somerford Park – and this time, it’s a much happier story. We’ll be hearing from Sadie after the prizegiving...

Yesterday, I caught up with German Olympian and FEI level 3 judge Sven Rothenberger, who’s been judged the PSG and inter I so far this week, to get his take on the standard on show at Somerford Park.

“I honestly never judged so many young horses at a national championship like here. You have quite a large amount of complete horses, elastic-moving horses, with very good talent, on a high level.

“With the first 10 or 12 horses in a range of two percent, it’s a very high level – not just one or two horses, several. Some had problems, some had highlights, but on average we have a very high quality of good young horses.

“I have to say the horse of Laura Tomlinson’s horse [Ostmarks Digal] seems to be a talent to take the weight and make the difficult movements later. I had the feeling that after every extended movement, she was able to do a very collected movement too – that showed me the horse really took the weight onto the hind legs, with the shoulders coming up, so it always had an uphill tendency.

“In the PSG I liked very much the horse of Fiona Bigwood [Newton Sylvanite], which was a little tense in the corner and lost a lot of points there, but had a lot of elasticity and a very strong hind leg.

“In the inter I there were horses like Becky Moody’s, who had mistakes, but if they don’t make the mistakes, they have high quality. Some had contact issues today – if those are solved, they might be fantastic horses in the future too.”

And we’re into the KBIS British Dressage five-year-old championship – a reminder of your finalists: Rowan Collins on Melody HC (Morricone x Danciano), Tom Goode on Dynamic Prince (Dynamic Dream x Foundation), and Sarah Millis on Toddington Reet Petite (Valverde x Lord Leatherdale).

I always feel like we could make more of these young horse championships – after the grand prix, they’re probably the biggest draw. Perhaps more horses in the final round, more prize money (top prize is currently £1,000), or an auction? I don’t know, might be a scheduling nightmare! But they’re a massive draw in Europe.

September 13, 2026 – 8:07 AM

Ride judge Phoebe Peters – who’s travelled over from where she’s based at Reesink Horses in Eibergen, the Netherlands – tries first, Toddington Reet Petite. Here's what she had to say:

“A really, really nice start – super rideable, workable horse. Obviously, they’re only five years old, and it’s quite a big atmosphere for them to be in, but she was really nice on my leg, really nice in the contact, really nice feeling.

“The Lord Leatherdale bloodline always gives the horses really super adjustability, and that was something you could already feel with her. She’s only five, but you can really feel the ability to go forward and trot on, and also already showing super collection in both paces.”

September 13, 2026 – 8:08 AM

Next she tries Tom Goode’s Dynamic Prince, who’s a little tentative to start with:

“Compared to the last one, who was quite short and compact in the body, this guy is big – a little more length in his body. You have to consider how that affects how the horses develop – a big horse like him probably needs a bit more time to develop the strength behind, to carry himself a bit more.

“But again, a really super feeling on him. He was a little unsure at the start – different rider, everything like that – but after a few rounds he adapted really nicely to my aids. In the canter, I had the feeling the adjustability was good; the trot maybe needs a bit more time, but also a really nice feeling.”

Asked what else she looks for beyond rideability when trying young horses, Phoebe explained: “Generally, with the young horses, I look more for the walk and the canter quality. The trot is more trainable – as long as the mechanics are good, a good hind leg, we can normally develop the trot a bit more. So having that really nice swing in the walk, relaxation through the back, and the canter a little uphill.

“I had moments with him in the canter where you could really feel he could bring that uphill balance. I think he'll develop into a really nice horse.”

Judge Spencer Wilton added his own thoughts on the gelding: “To reiterate what Phoebe’s just mentioned, a completely different type of horse – very tall, very elegant, extremely good-looking. You can see really rangy, big, ground-covering paces, and horses born like that just sometimes take a little longer to gain and learn adjustability, mainly through the fact that it just takes time for them to strengthen.

“But a super elegant horse, and really lovely to watch – very eye-catching, and fills the arena. He looks like he's going to have a very exciting future.”

September 13, 2026 – 8:11 AM

And finally, the ride of Rowan Collins’ Melody HC:

“It was really nice to feel – actually, as she got a bit more used to me, how relaxed the walk could get. She has a really nice feeling of swing from behind through the body in the walk, so I really liked that.

“In the canter, she already feels like she’s showing nice adjustability – you can ride forward and back very easily, she’s super balanced. Really good feeling.”

September 13, 2026 – 8:13 AM

And the results are in... Sarah Millis and Toddington Reet Petite (Valverde x Lord Leatherdale) take the five-year-old title, with Rowan Collins and Melody HC (Morricone x Danciano) second, and Tom Goode and Dynamic Prince (Dynamic Dream x Foundation) third.

September 13, 2026 – 8:51 AM

Under-21 champions on their winning rides

Amelia Dovey (children on horses), Sheepcote Jackson: “It feels surreal – I can’t believe what a year I’ve had, and how he felt in there.”

On taking over the ride from her sister: “It feels like there’s a lot of expectation, but at the same time, I just feel like if I ride my best, it doesn’t matter how it goes really.”

Amelia Goodear (pony riders), Furioso V.H. Enkershof: “He was such a good boy today,and I was so pleased. His half-passes, shoulder-in and simple changes were great – we’ve been working really hard on those.”

On her season: “It’s been unbelievable – we’ve had definite lows where we’ve not performed our best, but also highs, going to the Europeans and winning here. He’s made all my dreams come true this year.”

Abigail Gray (junior riders), Jack Diamond: “We didn’t have a clean test, we missed one of our changes, but we’re still getting to know each other. We’ve been together for four months, and we’re starting to see an improvement since our last test at Wellington.”

On taking over the ride from Becky Moody: “Becky was riding him before, and I’ve taken him down the levels. I’m from Aberdeen, but I’m currently taking a gap year training at Becky’s, helping warm up her horses.”

Myles Graham (young riders), Fred Astaire WD: “It was a joy to ride – every stride I enjoyed riding. He is a one-of-a-kind horse, and I’m super grateful to Dan Sherriff and Lindsay Roberts, the owners of Fred – I wouldn’t be on this journey without them.”

On his ambitions: “I’ve known from a very young age that this is what I want to do. I want to aspire to be on a senior team – that’s one of my lifelong dreams.”

September 13, 2026 – 8:58 AM

Sarah Millis on five-year-old champion Toddington Reet Petite:

“I’m really pleased with her, very proud of her. She’s actually out of a mare bred by a good friend of mine, Camilla Brogaard – she’s not a big breeder, but she had a nice mare and produced some nice foals. It’s like watching your baby grow up, and she showed herself so well today.

“I wasn’t expecting her to win the whole thing. I know her rideability and trainability, but the five-year-olds have been a really strong class this year, so I was just hoping she’d get through to the final – this was the icing on the cake.

“She was actually selected for the World Breeding Championships as a five-year-old and got through the selection at Wellington – but we felt it might be a bit too much too soon for her at this stage, so we didn’t take her there in the end. This is the biggest atmosphere she’s been in, and she's literally just soaked it all up.”

September 13, 2026 – 9:00 AM

Five-year-olds done and dusted – next up is the KBIS British Dressage six-year-old final. Your three finalists: Bryony Goodwin on Simply Secret (Secret x Waikiki), Lily Laughton on Viva Valentine (Viva Gold x Ampere), and Jezz Palmer on MS Broadway M (Bon Courage x Royal Classic) – who won the five-year-old title here last year.

September 13, 2026 – 9:35 AM

First to ride for Phoebe is the ride of Jezz Palmer – MS Broadway M (Bon Courage x Royal Classic) – who she also rode last year in the five-year-olds:

“It was really cool to feel how he’s developed since last year. Compared to the five-year-old, we’re looking for even more adjustability, the beginnings of taking more weight behind – especially in the canter, where I did a little easy working pirouette, just because his canter felt like I could ask for that. It was really nice to feel the development he’s made in the last year – he’s done a good job in terms of development.

“Last year he had a really big canter, with a lot of air time and power. What was really nice to feel now is that he has a lot more gears in the canter – I felt like I could really sit him back. You could already imagine feeling like you could go into a pirouette with him.

Sven Rothenberger, judging: “With this horse, it's a really impressive and expressive horse with a lot of dynamic – very good freedom of shoulder in trot and canter, a lot of uphill airtime in the canter. What Phoebe showed us, as she also mentioned, is that when you let him be a bit more in self-carriage, you can see this horse open up and present himself with real presence.

“But as always, where there’s light, there’s also a little to criticise. We liked the walk very much, and the canter, but in the trot, at times, the horse wasn’t perfectly balanced – perhaps it’s just a moment, but we have to make a decision today.

“Our other small criticism is that when he was stretching on a long rein, he was a little bit looking for his balance, and this needs to be developed more in the future – that this horse trots through the body and develops a bit more pushing power from behind, so the connection between the front and hindleg is a bit more solid.”

September 13, 2026 – 9:38 AM

And next is the ride of Lily Laughton – the stallion Viva Valentine (Viva Gold x Ampere) – who had the top-scoring canter yesterday:

Phoebe: “The canter gave a really super feeling – he has so much airtime, he’s uphill, he’s balanced. You can go forward; you can set him back already. His canter feels like it’s got so much scope, but also the ability to collect, which was a really good feeling.

“Compared to the last horse, this one’s a little bit smaller – Jezz’s horse is a really big, impressive horse, but then you feel the difference in adjustability. This one maybe doesn’t have as much power, maybe doesn’t have as impressive a front leg in the trot, but you could already feel really nice adjustability, and the ability to go sideways was really easy.”

Isobel Wessels, judging: “Outstanding, really outstanding – and I’d also like to congratulate Phoebe on doing such a good job. She was straight away working on those gears, the freedom and activity, ground cover, airtime – all the things we’re looking for, this horse has an abundance of. When Phoebe let the horse stretch at the end in the canter, you really saw the natural self-carriage, and this was quite exceptional.

“What I really appreciated was that Phoebe used this wonderful canter to improve the quality of the trot, so the trot gradually became less quick, more ground-covering, more elastic. The walk is phenomenally good. Overall, I just think it looked like a really lovely package.”

September 13, 2026 – 9:41 AM

And lastly, Phoebe rides Bryony Goodwin’s Simply Secret (Secret x Waikiki):

Asked about the key qualities she looks for in a horse with medal-winning potential, Phoebe said: “As I said with the five-year-olds, a lot of it is the character, the rideability, how workable you feel a horse is, the walk, and the quality of the canter.

“It’s the feeling of the horse's attitude in terms of his acceptance of the aids, and whether it’s something you think you can work with in the future.

“He’s a super well-trained horse, and I think that was also what impressed the judges yesterday. He’s really easy-going, really nice in the frame – you can feel that today; you can just ride him really nicely through the movements, through the transitions.”

September 13, 2026 – 9:44 AM

And the results are in from the six-year-old final... Lily Laughton and Viva Valentine (Viva Gold x Ampere) take the title, with Bryony Goodwin and Simply Secret (Secret x Waikiki) second and Jezz Palmer and MS Broadway M (Bon Courage x Royal Classic) third.

September 13, 2026 – 9:53 AM

Just under an hour until the big one – the Kudos grand prix freestyle gets under way at 3.10pm, with the overall national champion being crowned at the end of it.

That class is being live streamed, if you’d like to follow along with us, check out our guide on how to watch the National Dressage Championships.

September 13, 2026 – 9:57 AM

Jezz may have been third in the six-year-olds, but earlier today he won the Absolute Equestrian Collective preliminary gold on four-year-old Spotify Anmore (Las Vegas x Daily Diamond), scoring 75.93%. Here’s what he had to say:

“He’s only four, and he’d actually done the four-year-olds a couple of days before, so I was a bit worried he might be tired. He felt good in the warm-up, and he’d been a bit fresh in the four-year-old class, so I thought I’d do a little more with him in case he got distracted. But actually he was really calm today – which meant the transitions were good, and he let go through the walk more. The feeling he gives, at four years old, is unreal.

“We bought him in Holland – I’d tried a lot of horses out there, and I know the yard we got him from quite well. The first time I got on him, they said ‘Don't move’ – he was so sensitive, but it never felt ungenuine, it just felt like he was a bit scared.

“The lady who does our backing had him for six months, and honestly, he wouldn’t be where he is today without her. She got him trusting us, and now he’s very much one of those horses – if he knows you and trusts you, he’ll give you everything. If someone else gets on, he’s like, ‘Who are you?’ He’s very aware of who’s riding him.

“He was second in the four-year-olds to Fiona Bigwood, with a couple of big mistakes – he got a bit nervous, a bit tight and didn’t let go through the walk enough, which is exactly what I wanted to focus on today. He went in so excited today, like he already knew he’d got it.

“He’s got the biggest future – he has talent for all of it. Everyone who sees him wants to ride him. He’s a bit sensitive, but he’s never nasty, he just doesn’t have a nasty bone in his body. We’re really lucky to have found him – we get offers for him every week now.”

September 13, 2026 – 10:05 AM

Lily Laughton, on six-year-old champion Viva Valentine:

“Phenomenal. I didn’t really come here thinking he was going to win it – he’s still very inexperienced, he’s never seen anything like the main arena, so he was just so cool, he has the best head on him. I can’t ask for any more, so I’m very happy.

“He’s never seen anything like that atmosphere, and with Phoebe [Peters] it was a new rider on him too – I’m always the one who rides him – and he’s still young, so you never know how they’re going to react. But Phoebe is such an amazing rider – as soon as she got on him, I knew he’d be fine.

“Watching someone like her ride him was amazing, so cool – she’s one of the best riders in Britain, someone I looked up to when I was young going to ponies. For her to ride my horse in the finals was really special.

“The comments from the judges – especially Sven [Rothenberger], who’s come over from Germany were just amazing, we all cried, it’s more than I could have ever imagined.

“His canter is ridiculous – we call him mini-Glamourdale, he’s like a pint-sized version of him. I’m very excited for what’s to come. He finds everything so easy – he’s already starting piaffe, and as Phoebe said, you can bring him back and collect him, which you obviously need for grand prix. So I don’t see why he might not go all the way up – we’ll see.

“It’s been an amazing competition. All the horses have really exceeded my expectations.”

September 13, 2026 – 10:24 AM

Dannie Morgan on advanced medium gold winner Freya VII

Dannie Morgan’s third title of the week – on a third different horse – came in the advanced medium gold this morning, on seven-year-old Freya VII. He’d been sitting in the lead since an early draw, with a long wait to find out if it would hold:

“Really delighted with her – it’s always such a strong class, the advanced medium gold here. She’s just a seven-year-old, so probably one of the younger horses in the class, but she’s got a super temperament, she makes my job easy.

“She went round for a clear round and really gave her best shot – we were second in the arena this morning, so it was a long wait.”

On winning three titles now, on three different horses to be confirmed the championship’s leading rider: “I’m not actually finished yet, I’ve still got two more horses in the elementary gold, so we’ll have a go at that too.

“It’s been a great week, and I’m really delighted for my team and my owners – a lot goes into preparing the horses to come here, so it’s nice when you can pull off a few results.”

September 13, 2026 – 10:26 AM

We’ve also got the results in from the advanced medium silver in the Vector Arena:

1st: Katie Alexandra Scott – Liverpool KS (71.58%)

2nd: Anna Burns – San Isidro (69.72%)

3rd: Joe Roome – Acqua Marina Della Caccia (68.81%)

4th: John Norcross – Impulz W (68.75%)

5th: Alicia Laughton – Armada Bathsheba (68.75%)

September 13, 2026 – 11:07 AM

We’re into a break in the grand prix freestyle, and Alexander Harrison-West has surged into the lead:

1st: Alexander Harrison-West – Kickback (72.93%)

2nd: Kimberley Siddorn – Dutch Class (70.18%)

3rd: Olivia Oakeley – Full House (68.90%)

4th: Darren Hicks – Tramontana Tiger Feet (67.78%)

5th: Tom Goode – Furstenrausch PS (67.35%)

I’ll be with you every step of the way now for the final four...

September 13, 2026 – 11:23 AM

First in after the break is Ruby Hughes and Farrell – fourth in the grand prix on a solid 69.59%.

With up-beat dance music, featuring tracks from Kygo, and an ambitious floorplan, straight from passage into a near half-piaffe pirouette – but it doesn’t quite come off, with Farrell looking a bit hesitant.

The difference between his collected and working frames is impressive. Farrell takes a while to settle into his walk work, and there's a mistake in the canter pirouette – such a shame.

They score 67.86% – but a remarkable achievement to be doing that at just 18-years-old.

September 13, 2026 – 11:33 AM

Charlotte Dujardin next – this is her and Brave Heart’s first freestyle together. He looks like he could passage for days. The first piaffe is a little slow in and out if you’re being picky.

A fantastic extended trot down the centre line and he walk looks better today too. It’s just tiny things now – like the finer details of the transitions between movements – preventing some of the eights from being nines.

Fantastic pirouettes and ones on a curving line. Charlotte guns it on the the extended canter, though Brave Heart’s a touch wide behind in the piaffe.

This is going to be big – 79.4%!

September 13, 2026 – 11:45 AM

Fiona Bigwood and Donna Bella are next and produce a safe clear round – scoring 75.05% to go provisional second.

Not enough to catch Charlotte but I think Fiona will be delighted with that.

September 13, 2026 – 11:50 AM

Last-to-go Gareth Hughes and Mowgli-Olympia MC – the nine-year-old gelding looks to be a serious talent for the future.

It's 79.35% – an exceptional score in its own right, but a mistake in the changes still leaves them in third, a mark of just how strong this freestyle has been.

That confirms it: Charlotte has won the freestyle, and she's the 2026 national dressage champion!

September 13, 2026 – 11:52 AM

Here are the full results from the Kudos grand prix freestyle – and Charlotte Dujardin has taken it in some style again:

1st Charlotte Dujardin – Braveheart II (79.40%)

2nd Fiona Bigwood – Donna Bella (75.05%)

3rd Gareth Hughes – Mowgli-Olympia MC (73.95%)

4th Alexander Harrison-West – Kickback (72.93%)

5th Kimberley Siddorn – Dutch Class (70.18%)

6th Olivia Oakeley – Full House (68.90%)

7th Ruby Hughes – Farrell (67.83%)

8th Darren Hicks – Tramontana Tiger Feet (67.78%)

9th Tom Goode – Furstenrausch PS (67.35%)

10th Anne-Marie Cowan – Woodcroft Royal Charter (66.18%)

September 13, 2026 – 11:52 AM

Hang tight, we’ll have all the reaction from Charlotte to come...

September 13, 2026 – 12:37 PM

Charlotte Dujardin on winning the freestyle and the national title, on Brave Heart II:

“It feels very good – it was a nice end to the show, and the sun was shining, which is even better, so we didn’t get wet!”

"That's actually [Gio’s] music – the music I used at the Tokyo Olympics. All year I’ve been doing specials, focusing on that and the grand prix, and then I was thinking, oh no, I’m going to have to do a freestyle – what am I going to do?

“I thought, okay, I’ll have to use one I’ve already got, so I thought this might work. He’d literally never done the floorplan before – I just had to give it a go and see what happened, and that’s what happened.

“He got a bit ahead of the music at the start, so I was a touch too far ahead waiting for it, but he gave everything a really good go, and I was so proud of him – it’s a very technical, difficult test, lots coming in and out of it, piaffe pirouettes, changes on the curves.

“I just changed the end and didn’t do another piaffe pirouette – I think for him, he’s just done loads of it already. But I was really, really happy with him, no big mistakes, it just felt like a really good experience for him.

“He’s such a sweet horse, you can’t fault him – he comes out for the prize-giving and just stands there for everyone to pat him, have pictures, see him. The crowd, the spectators coming over for photos – it’s very, very nice. I’ve just had a really nice time.”

September 13, 2026 – 12:42 PM

And that’s a wrap on the 2026 National Dressage Championships – what a ride. We’ve had all the seasons condensed into four days, but we’re closing out under beautiful sunshine.

Thank you for following along all week – it’s been a genuine pleasure bringing you all of it. See you at the next one.

Today’s winners:

Absolute Equestrian Collective prelim gold: Jezz Palmer – Spotify Anmore (75.93%)

KBIS young horse final, five-year-olds: Sarah Millis – Toddington Reet Petite (Valverde x Lord Leatherdale)

KBIS young horse final, six-year-olds: Lily Laughton – Viva Valentine (Viva Gold x Ampere)

British Dressage advanced medium gold: Dannie Morgan – Freya VII (71.64%)

British Dressage advanced medium silver: Katie Alexandra Scott – Liverpool KS (71.58%)

Under-21 Championship, Children on Horses: Amelia Dovey – Sheepcote Jackson (77.93%)

Under-21 Championship, Pony Riders: Amelia Goodear – Furioso V.H. Enkershof (69.62%)

Under-21 Championship, Junior Riders: Abigail Gray – Jack Diamond (68.89%)

Under-21 Championship, Young Riders: Myles Graham – Fred Astaire WD (71.81%)

Kudos grand prix freestyle gold, and 2026 national dressage champion: Charlotte Dujardin – Braveheart II (79.4%)

item.title: Meet the horse bought for £1 who overcame kissing spines – and a broken leg – and is competing at the national championships
item.dc:content:
Meet the horse bought for £1 who went from throwing people off to kissing spines surgery to the LeMieux National Dressage Championships – having recovered from a broken leg along the way.

Heather Bennett’s 10-year-old Hawtins Figaro is due to compete at elementary and medium level with Craig Messenger this week (10-13 September), and had also qualified for the para finals with Heather.

The competition comes two years after Heather bought him.

“I got him from another para rider; he’d had her off and injured her quite badly, and he had her trainer off too,” she told H&H. “She told me what had happened and I said it sounded like kissing spines.”

Heather had to wait until her vet Tim Booth was available, and he confirmed her suspicions.

“He said ‘Yes, kissing spines but it’s fixable’,” she said.

“My history has been that I’ve taken everyone’s cast-offs. I’m not a rich person so I’ve got to make good of what I ride. My friend had said he had the nicest temperament and [asked] why was he suddenly exploding. You find horses like this can get pushed from pillar to post and no one actually looks at the horse and asks what’s happening with it.

“I’ve had a few with kissing spines; I rehabbed another one and won the winter championships with him. But with kissing spines, it’s not about the surgery, it’s all about the rehab, and many people don’t have the knowledge or the time or the inclination to do it properly.”

Heather took her time, and after initial box rest for “Fig”, followed by groundwork and a slow build-up with frequent physio treatment, started competing him last summer, and qualified for the 2025 nationals.

“I brought him home and it was a lovely day so I put him out in the field,” she said.

“When I brought him in, he was on three legs.”

Fig had managed to break his splint bone, by “messing about in the field”, as was confirmed when Heather took him straight to the vet.

“Luckily it didn’t need surgery, so it was just time – and rest again,” she said. “He’s quite sharp and likes to keep his brain occupied so box rest is a challenge. He’s such a sweet horse but his brain’s very reactive.”

Heather had also had some health issues so about six months ago, she asked Craig and Dan Watson at Aster Horses to take him on.

Craig told H&H Hawtins Figaro is “very sharp but very lovely”.

“He was strong enough, he’d had enough time, his back was fine, his leg was fine,” Craig said. “He’s always a bit cheeky but within six months,we’ve gone from nothing to medium, and now we’ve qualified for the nationals.”

Fig and Heather also won the grade IV at the Hickstead CDI in May, which Dan and Craig organised.

“He thinks he knows best but he’s a really nice horse with a lovely temperament,” Craig said. “He’s very quick-minded so we can do pirouettes and changes; he’d probably do prix st georges next year. We’re looking forward to the nationals.”

Heather added that she has been unable to travel to Somerford to compete but will be cheering Craig and Fig on.

“I’m not sure I’ll actually be able to watch!” she said. “But at least he’s still going, I’m glad Craig is taking him.

“He’s a character. He loves people, he loves his treats and he’s very vocal when he sees you; he’s a sweetheart and the best pound I’ve spent – plus the interest!”

To stay up to date with the latest news and reports throughout the LeMieux National Dressage Championships, subscribe to the Horse & Hound website
item.description: Hawtins Figaro had just come back into work after his surgery and rehab when he was injured – and recovered again
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Jones
item.dc:description: <p>Eleanor joined <em>Horse & Hound</em> as news editor in March 2016, having spent eight and a half years working for local and national newspapers. During her time with <em>H&H</em>, Eleanor has attended numerous industry conferences and events, including the FEI sport forum, the British Equine Veterinary Association annual congress and the National Equine Forum, and has spoken at the NEF and the Saddle Research Trust conference. </p><p>She has reported on all disciplines and aspects of the industry, from Brexit to anti-bullying campaigns and from dressage rules to dressage mules. She spent time travelling across Europe with World Horse Welfare to see first-hand the experience of horses being transported thousands of miles to slaughter, producing reports for print, online and in video format, and has also reported on showjumping events from national qualifiers to international grands prix, as well as the 2021, 2023 and 2025 Europeans and 2022 World Championships.</p><p>Eleanor has been riding since she was seven, and was given her first pony, a £300 Welsh section B mare, at the age of 12. She worked for dressage and showjumping riders, and now has two warmblood mares who she competes at British Showjumping events, and two home-bred youngsters. She has competed in dressage but since her mark sheets have contained phrases such as “unexpected manoeuvre between C and M” and “well sat”, tends to stick to the jumping.</p>

Fig and Heather also won the grade IV at the Hickstead CDI in May, which Dan and Craig organised.

“He thinks he knows best but he’s a really nice horse with a lovely temperament,” Craig said. “He’s very quick-minded so we can do pirouettes and changes; he’d probably do prix st georges next year. We’re looking forward to the nationals.”

Heather added that she has been unable to travel to Somerford to compete but will be cheering Craig and Fig on.

“I’m not sure I’ll actually be able to watch!” she said. “But at least he’s still going, I’m glad Craig is taking him.

“He’s a character. He loves people, he loves his treats and he’s very vocal when he sees you; he’s a sweetheart and the best pound I’ve spent – plus the interest!”

item.title: Olympic rider suspended for 18 months maintains whip use caught on video was ‘last-chance rescue’ of a dangerous horse
item.dc:content:
An Olympic rider caught on video repeatedly hitting a horse has been suspended for 18 months by the FEI Tribunal.

Heath Ryan, 68, was found to have abused the horse – which he consistently denied – and fined CHF 3,000 (£2,700) as a result of the footage, which emerged last summer.

H&H reported at the time that Heath said he was sad about the “awful” video of the session – which he described as part of a “rescue mission”.

This was his case to the FEI Tribunal; he said he was helping a friend with a horse who had become dangerous, and that the footage covered about 60 seconds of a 45-minute “remedial training session undertaken to re-educate the horse out of a demonstrated pattern of dangerous conflict behaviour”.

Heath represented Australia at the 2008 Olympics in dressage and was eventing at four-star level in 2024. He said he had spent over 50 years training and rehabilitating horses, coaching riders from beginners to the Thai Asian Games eventing team, and the Australian Olympic gold medal-winning team.

“He highlighted the longevity of horses under his care, citing specific competition results at advanced ages, and stated that results of this calibre could not be achieved by abusing horses,” the Tribunal report states.

“The person who recorded the videos had left his training establishment prior to releasing them and, before doing so, had signed over two horses to his ownership because they were too difficult for her to ride. It was widely accepted that the motivation for the video release was vindictive, and that this had been made known to the FEI during investigative interviews which had not been disclosed to the Tribunal.”

Heath said the horse had been sent to three people to back, unsuccessfully. The horse was returned as dangerous, and seriously injured his owner. She approached Heath to train him, adding that if he could not help she would put the horse down.

Heath Ryan said he used equitation science principles

He said he used equitation science principles of negative reinforcement with progressive escalation of aids, that he used the whip carefully, “and he was careful not to cross into a fear state”, and that this horse was a “highly unusual case”.

Character witnesses for Heath included Olympic eventer Boyd Martin, who had known him 30 years, and said he does not abuse horses.

“He had never seen him lose his temper or use anger, force or fear,” the report states. “In his view, the horse in the video was a last-chance rescue of an animal facing destruction after it had attacked its rider, and the respondent succeeded where other trainers had failed.

“He stated that the video was edited and weaponised by someone with a grudge unrelated to horse welfare. The audio appeared exaggerated and likely manipulated.”

Olympic rider Vicki Roycroft agreed, as did vet Belinda Flynn. Former Equestrian Australia chair and Olympian Wayne Roycroft said he was “initially concerned by the video [but] the context was a horse that had seriously injured its owner and faced euthanasia”, and the horse had since been ridden without incident.

“The methodology was successful,” the report states of Heath’s submissions. “The horse responded during the session. It was subsequently re-educated, re-homed and is now ridden successfully. This demonstrated that the use of the whip had not been excessive.”

The FEI case

The FEI said there was no proof the horse had been dangerous.

“On the alleged abuse, the FEI relied on the expert report of Dr Rachel Murray,” the report states.

“Dr Murray concluded that the respondent whipped the horse excessively during the training session… identifying at least 41 whip strikes in approximately 31 seconds in the first video and nine in the second, applied with high force in a forehand technique to a sensitive area of the flank and lumbar region, without release or reward.

“Dr Murray further observed multiple behavioural signs of pain, distress and conflict in the horse, together with signs of left-hindlimb instability and possible lameness or an underlying veterinary issue and concluded that repeatedly whipping a horse that may be in pain is not an acceptable training method and amounts to abuse.

“The FEI submitted that Dr Murray’s report rebutted the respondent’s contention that the use of the whip was justified as the FEI-recognised equitation science methodology, noting that any ethically applied aversive stimulus must be no more than an irritant and that pain should be ruled out before conflict behaviour is addressed through training.”

Ryan Heath did not show anger

The panel found that Heath did not show anger or temper, nor did he escalate beyond hitting the horse on the quarters in response to the evasion and kicking out. The panel agreed that the second video showed that the whip use stopped when the horse went forward, after which the horse was seen trotting around the arena,

“Whatever the horse’s history and the respondent’s undoubted experience, the videos depict aggressive use of the whip to overcome the horse’s resistance,” the report states. “While the respondent may have genuinely believed that his training technique and use of the whip were necessary and appropriate given the context in which the horse came to him and its established resistances, the evidence provided shows that the use of the whip was excessive.”

The panel found abuse was committed, “even if his intentions for rehabilitation were good”, and that the footage brought the FEI and horse sport into disrepute.

In deciding the sanction, the panel considered Heath’s unblemished record over many years, the fact it was one horse on one occasion, “that it appeared to be a measured if misguided attempt to overcome the horse’s kicking resistance”, and the “substantial support expressed by members of the Australian equestrian community”.

It also cited the “gravity of the conduct”, and the fact Heath did not recognise “the harshness of the images depicted in the evidence”.

Heath’s suspension runs from its provisional start last June until this December. He was also ordered to pay the FEI’s 3,000 CHF legal costs.

item.dc:description: <p>Eleanor joined <em>Horse & Hound</em> as news editor in March 2016, having spent eight and a half years working for local and national newspapers. During her time with <em>H&H</em>, Eleanor has attended numerous industry conferences and events, including the FEI sport forum, the British Equine Veterinary Association annual congress and the National Equine Forum, and has spoken at the NEF and the Saddle Research Trust conference. </p><p>She has reported on all disciplines and aspects of the industry, from Brexit to anti-bullying campaigns and from dressage rules to dressage mules. She spent time travelling across Europe with World Horse Welfare to see first-hand the experience of horses being transported thousands of miles to slaughter, producing reports for print, online and in video format, and has also reported on showjumping events from national qualifiers to international grands prix, as well as the 2021, 2023 and 2025 Europeans and 2022 World Championships.</p><p>Eleanor has been riding since she was seven, and was given her first pony, a £300 Welsh section B mare, at the age of 12. She worked for dressage and showjumping riders, and now has two warmblood mares who she competes at British Showjumping events, and two home-bred youngsters. She has competed in dressage but since her mark sheets have contained phrases such as “unexpected manoeuvre between C and M” and “well sat”, tends to stick to the jumping.</p>

item.title: Which nations secured Olympic and Paralympic dressage qualification at the World Championships – and who missed out?
item.dc:content:
Fourteen nations secured Olympic or Paralympic dressage qualification for the 2028 Games in LA in the two team finals at the 2026 World Dressage Championships in Aachen.

In the Olympic dressage team final, the top six ranked teams – Germany, Britain, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Sweden – all booked their tickets to Los Angeles, alongside the hosts, the US (eighth), who qualified automatically.

For the complete breakdown of scores across all 19 dressage teams, see our full grand prix results.

For Britain’s Carl Hester, qualification mattered more than the colour of the medal. “We’re trying to qualify for the Olympic Games and pave the way for the next few years for new combinations to come along,” he said. “That feeling of relief is huge.”

A seventh nation also secured a dressage berth through a separate route: as the highest-placed team from FEI Group G (covering southeast Asia and Oceania), Australia claimed the one quota reserved for that region, finishing 13th overall. Thailand, the only other Group G nation fielding a full team in Aachen, missed out.

Portugal were the nation left to rue what got away in the main quota pool, finishing seventh on 212.625 – short of Sweden’s sixth-placed 216.552. Along with the other European nations outside the qualifying places, they will get a second chance at the 2027 European Championships in Randbøl, Denmark, where the three highest-ranked teams not already qualified will pick up the remaining places.

Canada finished just 0.062 points behind the USA’s team total in ninth. They will get another shot at Olympic qualification at the 2027 Pan American Games in Lima, Peru, where a top-two finish – with the qualified US excluded from contention – will guarantee a place.

As qualification was not on the line, the US had the freedom to blood inexperienced combinations rather than chase a result. Late call-up Megan Davies (Toronto Lightfoot) had barely a day’s notice before replacing Geñay Vaughn (Gino).

“I got the call Saturday night at 5 o’clock saying we were going,” she said. “We were ready to hit the road at 7.30 in the morning the next day.”

Both she and her horse were newcomers to the big stage – “This is his first big event... everything is sort of a new experience with the two of us, and this is my first big one too” – part of a deliberate strategy from the team. “They put in a couple of green combinations and let us get our footing,” she explained.

Whether that gamble pays off is another matter. For all the high-fives and optimism radiating from the US camp, it would be a surprise to see any of these combinations line up in LA – and you suspect an eighth-place finish there wouldn’t be met with quite the same magnanimity. The hope will be that some of their big-money buys, like Indian Rock and Bohemian, both absent from Aachen, come good and stay sound.

Para dressage: who’s heading to LA28

While the able-bodied US team used the freedom to blood green combinations and settled for eighth, the para dressage team treated it as no excuse to ease off, winning team gold on a record-breaking score under chef d’équipe Michel Assouline. If anything, the pressure felt higher, not lower, he explained:

“It’s an important Games for Team USA because it's a home Games, but we also know that a home Games is even more pressure, because the team at home will expect even more,” he said.

“I’m still very confident we have a system in place that works. We’ve worked hard on putting a strategy together with strong foundations, so I have a solid roadmap.”

Seven tickets for LA28 were up for grabs behind them. Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, Great Britain, Italy, France and Sweden all secured their places; Britain’s fifth-placed finish was enough to seal qualification although it missed out on the team podium.

British para performance manager Georgina Sharples was left with mixed emotions. “I’m thrilled that we have qualified – coming here to qualify for LA 2028 was the primary aim, and we’ve achieved that," she said. “But I’m disappointed with the final results... we very much came here with an expectation that we'd medal as a team too. We’ve got some cracking horses, and they delivered some super work, but we also had some incredibly expensive spooks. You can’t get away with that at this level.”

Looking ahead to LA, she was keen to stress the positives: "Our riders are all very much on an upward trajectory. We’re still assessing horsepower... You need competitions like this, where the pressure is high, to give those riders that exposure. I think we’ll take a huge amount of positives from here and build on it.”

Teams who secured dressage Olympic qualification in Aachen

  • Germany
  • Great Britain
  • Denmark
  • Belgium
  • Netherlands
  • Sweden
  • Australia (Group G)
  • USA – already qualified as hosts

Teams who secured para dressage Paralympic qualification in Aachen

  • Germany
  • Netherlands
  • Denmark
  • Great Britain
  • Italy
  • France
  • Sweden
  • USA – already qualified as hosts
  • To stay up to date with all the breaking equestrian news throughout the year, subscribe to the Horse & Hound website

item.dc:creator: Oscar Williams
item.dc:description: <p>Oscar joined <em>Horse & Hound</em> in October 2023 and is the magazine’s dressage editor and sports manager, overseeing coverage of equestrian sport.</p><p>Raised in Lancashire, Oscar started riding aged 12 and quickly became hooked. A keen member of the Lancaster & District branch of the Pony Club, he learnt to ride on a succession of hand-me-down ponies before persuading his parents to buy him his own horse – a wholly unsuitable but much-loved Welsh section C.</p><p>Oscar went on to study equine science at Myerscough College and, after deciding jumping wasn’t his strong suit, turned to dressage. Inspired by the London 2012 Olympics, he later spent four years working for leading trainer Emile Faurie. During that time, he competed at the 2015 National Dressage Championships and travelled with the yard to CDIs at Aachen, Vidauban, Saumur and Achleiten.</p><p>He also holds a master’s degree in Literature from York St John University (2021), combining his equestrian background with a passion for writing about the sport.</p><p>He regularly reports on elite dressage, breeding and welfare issues, as well as the science and policy shaping modern equestrian sport.</p><p>Oscar now lives in Cumbria with his two boisterous spaniels, Miffy and Dougal, and is interested in making equestrian sport more inclusive and accessible.</p>

item.title: Can you define horse-rider harmony – and how do we measure it? Experts debate
item.dc:content:
Discussions are ongoing in the dressage world around how to describe harmony.

H&H reported that among the 2027 FEI rule changes proposed in dressage, British Dressage (BD) – via British Equestrian – had called for a “clear definition of harmony” (news, 6 August).

BD CEO Jason Brautigam told H&H “harmony is fundamental to the object of dressage”.

“The object is the development of the horse as a happy athlete through harmonious education, allowing the horse to be loose and flexible but confident and keen, achieving understanding with the rider,” he said.

“These qualities are revealed by the partnership between horse and rider and measured in performance; through the paces, movements, engagement of the hindquarters, originating from impulsion and without tension or resistance.

“That gives us a clearer basis for describing harmony in practice. The challenge is to ensure this is articulated clearly enough that judges know what they are looking for, and riders and coaches understand what they should be seeking. If we want to encourage harmonious riding, the judging needs to recognise and reward it consistently.”

Mr Brautigam added that BD believes harmony should be assessed in individual movements, rather than a general impression or collective mark, and reflect movement quality and how it is achieved.

“Rather than reintroducing another collective, we believe the aim should be to embed harmony within the assessment of the performance itself,” he said.

“Harmony should not be treated as an additional aesthetic alongside the fundamentals of dressage. It is integral; the harmonious education of the horse in a positive mental and physical state, resulting in a confident and willing athlete.”

Mr Brautigam said the next step is “a clear and usable definition”, then to ensure judging reflects this throughout the test.

“The proposed changes to FEI rules, and review of tests that will follow, provide us with the opportunity to achieve this,” he said.

International dressage judge Isobel Wessels told H&H good judges, riders and trainers know what harmony is.

“Everyone has their own measure of harmony; in countries that don’t have a history of horse sport it might be more difficult to put a heading to it, but I do believe most dressage people recognise harmony when they see it,” she said.

“For me, harmony is when the horse goes seamlessly from one movement to the next with lightness and from small aids. That shows a willingness to work with the rider – but if the rider isn’t asking anything, that’s no good either.

“As judges, we read the horse from the moment it goes around the edge of the arena. If a horse spooks at something, for me that isn’t lack of harmony, it’s a live animal reacting to the environment. But if I see a horse reacting in a negative way because he’s stressed or the rider isn’t very competent, I come down on the mark and comment accordingly.”

Isobel added that judges follow FEI rules and attend annual training and exams.

“If anybody has sat in the judges' box and seen how many seconds you have to give a comment and mark, without falling behind, it’s an enormous task and we’re all very conscious of the influence we have,” she said.

“This word ‘harmony’ has always been in the front of our minds. It’s nothing new, it has always been part of the training scale, that’s not one person’s opinion – it’s part of the manual we follow to be able to ride, train and judge.”

International animal welfare consultant Natalie Waran said a definition of harmony is “only useful if it leads to something that can be seen, described and agreed on”.

“That is why measurement matters. It doesn’t replace the judgement of experienced horse people but it gives that judgement something solid to work from, and several parts of what is termed ‘harmony’ can now be assessed in this way,” said Professor Waran.

Professor Waran said evidence suggests harmony can be “defined well enough to be scored”, if it is “treated as more than aesthetic impression”.

“Describing it as the interaction between communication, the behaviour and affective state of the horse, biomechanical function and longer-term welfare outcomes makes it possible to define, teach and increasingly measure the qualities that sit underneath a successful performance,” she said.

“Seen that way, harmony isn’t an indefinable artistic ideal but an evidence-informed feature of good horsemanship, and one that can be assessed fairly when science is there to support it.”

  • To stay up to date with the latest from Burghley, subscribe to the Horse & Hound website

item.dc:creator: Becky Murray
item.dc:description: <p>Becky Murray started freelance writing for <em>Horse & Hound</em> in 2016 alongside other equestrian titles, before joining the <em>H&H</em> news team in July 2018. She moved up to senior news writer in January 2022. During her time at <em>H&H</em> she has reported on a broad range of topics across the equestrian industry including welfare issues, veterinary studies, FEI Tribunal hearings, rider safety, and road safety campaigns. In 2019 she attended the national Strangles Symposium and the Scottish welfare conference.</p><p>Becky was part of the home remote reporting team for the Tokyo and Paris Olympic Games as well as multiple European Championships. She has reported in person from Morris Equestrian, the Royal Highland Show, Blair Castle, Scone Palace and Luhmühlen. She is attending the 2025 European Para Dressage Championships as Horse & Hound’s on-site reporter.</p><p>Based in north Scotland, Becky learnt to ride at the age of five. She got the showjumping bug with her 13.2hh older pony Phoenix, who used to particularly enjoy a chase-me-Charlie. She went on to compete in British Showjumping and riding club activities as a teenager with her pony Sparkle. After losing two horses in 2015 to illness and injury, Becky is now producing two Irish mares, Ruby and Chloe, and hopes to get back in the showjumping ring in the future. She also has two miniature Shetland sisters, Mootie and Poppet, who keep her on her toes.</p>

“That gives us a clearer basis for describing harmony in practice. The challenge is to ensure this is articulated clearly enough that judges know what they are looking for, and riders and coaches understand what they should be seeking. If we want to encourage harmonious riding, the judging needs to recognise and reward it consistently.”

Mr Brautigam added that BD believes harmony should be assessed in individual movements, rather than a general impression or collective mark, and reflect movement quality and how it is achieved.

“Rather than reintroducing another collective, we believe the aim should be to embed harmony within the assessment of the performance itself,” he said.

“Harmony should not be treated as an additional aesthetic alongside the fundamentals of dressage. It is integral; the harmonious education of the horse in a positive mental and physical state, resulting in a confident and willing athlete.”

Mr Brautigam said the next step is “a clear and usable definition”, then to ensure judging reflects this throughout the test.

“The proposed changes to FEI rules, and review of tests that will follow, provide us with the opportunity to achieve this,” he said.

International dressage judge Isobel Wessels told H&H good judges, riders and trainers know what harmony is.

“Everyone has their own measure of harmony; in countries that don’t have a history of horse sport it might be more difficult to put a heading to it, but I do believe most dressage people recognise harmony when they see it,” she said.

“For me, harmony is when the horse goes seamlessly from one movement to the next with lightness and from small aids. That shows a willingness to work with the rider – but if the rider isn’t asking anything, that’s no good either.

“As judges, we read the horse from the moment it goes around the edge of the arena. If a horse spooks at something, for me that isn’t lack of harmony, it’s a live animal reacting to the environment. But if I see a horse reacting in a negative way because he’s stressed or the rider isn’t very competent, I come down on the mark and comment accordingly.”

Isobel added that judges follow FEI rules and attend annual training and exams.

“If anybody has sat in the judges' box and seen how many seconds you have to give a comment and mark, without falling behind, it’s an enormous task and we’re all very conscious of the influence we have,” she said.

“This word ‘harmony’ has always been in the front of our minds. It’s nothing new, it has always been part of the training scale, that’s not one person’s opinion – it’s part of the manual we follow to be able to ride, train and judge.”

International animal welfare consultant Natalie Waran said a definition of harmony is “only useful if it leads to something that can be seen, described and agreed on”.

“That is why measurement matters. It doesn’t replace the judgement of experienced horse people but it gives that judgement something solid to work from, and several parts of what is termed ‘harmony’ can now be assessed in this way,” said Professor Waran.

Professor Waran said evidence suggests harmony can be “defined well enough to be scored”, if it is “treated as more than aesthetic impression”.

“Describing it as the interaction between communication, the behaviour and affective state of the horse, biomechanical function and longer-term welfare outcomes makes it possible to define, teach and increasingly measure the qualities that sit underneath a successful performance,” she said.

“Seen that way, harmony isn’t an indefinable artistic ideal but an evidence-informed feature of good horsemanship, and one that can be assessed fairly when science is there to support it.”
